name: Classic-Style Test 4
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Fitness columnist: Our magazine’s website invited readers to report whether taking ice baths after hard workouts reduced their muscle soreness. Of the 900 readers who responded, 85 percent said that ice baths helped. So most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the fitness columnist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that athletes may be able to reduce muscle soreness in ways other than taking ice baths
draws a conclusion about athletes in general from a group of respondents who decided for themselves whether to take part
presumes, without providing justification, that athletes who feel less sore after workouts also perform better
takes for granted that because ice baths help most athletes, they help every athlete who takes them
criticizes ice baths on the grounds that some of the readers who responded did not benefit from them
questions.explanation: The 900 respondents are magazine readers who chose to write in, and readers who got relief are the ones most motivated to report it, so they may not represent athletes generally; (B) names this self-selected sample. (A) is tempting because it sounds like a missed alternative, but the argument says nothing about ice baths being the only remedy, so other remedies don’t matter. (D) describes an overgeneralization the columnist never makes; the conclusion says ‘most,’ not ‘every.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85 percent of the 900 website readers who chose to respond said ice baths helped.

breakdown.analysis: Who answers a ‘did ice baths help you?’ call on a fitness website? Mostly people who use ice baths and liked them. People who tried them, felt nothing, and moved on rarely bother to write in. That’s a self-selected sample, a classic sampling flaw; know it. It’s like a restaurant asking diners to post reviews and concluding most diners loved it because 85 percent of the reviews are glowing. We need an answer that says the sample picked itself and may not match athletes in general.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The columnist never says ice baths are the only way to reduce soreness. Other remedies existing doesn’t touch whether ice baths work for most athletes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Stretching reduces soreness, so stretching is the only thing athletes need to recover from hard workouts.

choices.note: CORRECT. The respondents volunteered, and people with good results are more likely to report them. A website readership that chose to answer can’t stand in for ‘most athletes.’
The argument never mentions performance. It’s only about feeling less sore. This answer adds a link the columnist didn’t make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Athletes who take ice baths feel less sore, so ice baths must make them run faster.

choices.note: Too strong a description. The conclusion says ‘most athletes,’ not every athlete. The columnist doesn’t overgeneralize to each individual.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ice baths relieve soreness for most athletes, so they will certainly relieve yours.

choices.note: Opposite of what happens. The columnist praises ice baths; nothing in the argument criticizes them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Fifteen percent of readers said ice baths didn’t help, so ice baths are worthless.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: For most of the last century, Halvern’s downtown streets were laid out as one-way pairs designed to move commuter traffic quickly. Several nearby cities have recently converted such streets back to two-way traffic. Halvern should do the same with Pike and Orrin Streets. Most commuters now use the new bypass, so the one-way design no longer serves its original purpose, and two-way streets slow cars enough to make the sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the urban planner’s argument?
choices: Halvern’s downtown streets were designed as one-way pairs in order to move commuter traffic quickly.
Several cities near Halvern have recently converted one-way streets back to two-way traffic.
The one-way design of Halvern’s downtown streets no longer serves the purpose for which it was adopted.
Pike and Orrin Streets in Halvern ought to be converted to two-way traffic.
Two-way streets slow cars enough to make downtown sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.
questions.explanation: Everything in the argument supports the recommendation that Halvern convert Pike and Orrin Streets to two-way traffic, which (D) restates. (C) is tempting because it is itself drawn from the fact that commuters use the bypass, but it is only a step toward the recommendation. (A) and (B) are background, and (E) is a supporting premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halvern should convert Pike and Orrin Streets to two-way traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Commuters now use the bypass, so the one-way design no longer serves its purpose; two-way streets slow cars and make sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first two sentences are background: history and what other cities did. They don’t argue for anything; you can ignore them. The third sentence, ‘Halvern should do the same,’ is the recommendation, and the last sentence gives the reasons for it. Note the conclusion sits in the middle, not at the end. We need an answer that says Pike and Orrin should become two-way.

choices.note: Background. This is just history about why the streets were built one-way. It supports nothing.
Background again. Other cities’ choices set the scene, but the planner doesn’t even use them as evidence.

Tempting, because it follows from ‘most commuters now use the bypass,’ so it looks like a conclusion. But it’s an intermediate step: it exists to support the recommendation, so it isn’t the main point.
CORRECT. ‘Halvern should do the same with Pike and Orrin Streets’ is what every other claim is there to support.
A premise. It’s one of the two reasons offered for converting the streets.

questions.stimulus: Since the thermostat on Tavola Pizzeria’s only oven began malfunctioning, causing the oven to run considerably hotter than its setting, the restaurant has had to throw out many overcooked trays of roasted vegetables. Yet over the same period, customers have rated Tavola’s pizza crusts much more highly than before, even though the pizzas are baked in the same oven.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Tavola’s pizza recipe calls for an oven temperature well below the temperature at which pizza crust crisps and browns best.
Since the malfunction began, Tavola’s cooks have been checking pizzas more often while they bake.
Customers who order pizza at Tavola seldom order roasted vegetables.
Tavola has raised the prices on its menu to cover the cost of the vegetables it has had to discard.
Many pizzerias use separate ovens for pizzas and for roasted dishes.
questions.explanation: If the recipe’s set temperature was too low for an ideal crust, an oven running hotter than its setting would push pizzas closer to the best temperature while overshooting for vegetables, so the defect helps the crust; that is (A). (B) is tempting, but checking more often could at most keep pizzas from burning; it doesn’t explain why crusts got better than before. (C), (D), and (E) don’t address why the same overheating improved the pizza.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The oven runs too hot and ruins vegetables, but pizzas from the same oven are now rated better than before.

breakdown.analysis: How can a broken oven make anything better? Only if the old temperature was wrong for pizza in the first place. Then ‘too hot’ for vegetables could be ‘just right’ for crust. It’s like a car whose speedometer reads low: a driver who always went too slow suddenly arrives on time. We need an answer showing the extra heat moves pizza toward its ideal, not away from it.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the recipe’s temperature was below the best crust temperature, the extra heat fixes the crust while still overcooking the vegetables. The defect turns out to help.

Tempting, because it shows the cooks reacting to the problem. But extra checking could only prevent burned pizzas. It doesn’t explain why crusts are rated better than they were before the malfunction.
Irrelevant. Who orders what doesn’t change what the oven does to the pizza.
Prices are a different dimension. This explains nothing about how the crusts improved.
Right topic, wrong group. Tavola uses one oven for both; what other pizzerias do is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: At the Brannock reservoir, swallows nesting under the high eaves of the old pump house fledge far more chicks per nest than do swallows nesting under the low footbridge nearby. Rats from the reservoir bank can easily climb to nests under the footbridge but not to those under the pump-house eaves. So predation by rats probably accounts for the difference.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ornithologist’s argument?
choices: Swallows at the pump house tend to lay their eggs earlier in the season than do swallows at the footbridge.
Rats are known to eat the eggs and nestlings of many kinds of birds.
Footbridge nests that were fitted with rat guards last year fledged about as many chicks per nest as pump-house nests did.
Far more people walk past the footbridge nests each day than walk past the pump-house nests.
Some swallows that nest at the pump house in one year nest at the footbridge in the next.
questions.explanation: If footbridge nests protected from rats do as well as pump-house nests, the location itself isn’t the problem and rats are, which strongly supports the causal claim; that is (C). (B) is tempting but only shows rats can eat nestlings in general, not that they explain this difference. (A) and (D) offer alternative causes and so weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rat predation probably explains why footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks than pump-house nests.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks; rats can reach footbridge nests but not pump-house nests.

breakdown.analysis: Rats can reach the footbridge nests, sure. But lots of things differ between a low footbridge and high eaves: people, noise, timing, shade. How do we know it’s the rats? The best support is a test: take away the rats and see if the difference disappears. We need an answer that isolates rats as the cause or rules out the other differences.

choices.note: This hands you an alternative cause: earlier breeders might simply do better. That weakens the argument.
Tempting, because it shows rats can do the damage. But ‘rats eat many birds’ eggs’ is general. It doesn’t show rats are what explains this particular gap.
CORRECT. Same footbridge, rats blocked, and the nests do as well as the pump-house nests. That pins the difference on rats rather than on the location itself.
Another alternative cause: human disturbance could be what hurts the footbridge nests. That weakens.
Irrelevant. Birds switching sites from year to year doesn’t tell you why one site fledges fewer chicks.

questions.stimulus:
Moreno: The warehouse workers’ union should accept the company’s contract offer. It raises wages 4 percent a year for three years, which is more than workers at any other warehouse in the region received in their most recent contracts.

Lyle: That raise is certainly generous. But the offer also lets the company require overtime on only one day’s notice, and workers with young children cannot arrange child care that quickly. The union should reject the offer unless that clause is removed.
questions.stem: Moreno and Lyle disagree over whether
choices: the wage increase in the company’s offer is larger than the increases recently received by other warehouse workers in the region
workers with young children would have difficulty arranging child care on one day’s notice
the size of the wage increase is the most important feature of any contract offer
the company would agree to remove the overtime clause from its offer
the union should accept the company’s offer in its current form
questions.explanation: Moreno says the union should accept the offer as made, while Lyle says it should be rejected unless the overtime clause comes out, so they disagree about accepting the offer in its current form, (E). (A) is tempting, but Lyle concedes the raise is generous and never disputes the regional comparison. Moreno says nothing about child care (B) or about which feature matters most (C), and neither speaker predicts what the company will do (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Moreno: accept the offer, because the raise beats every other warehouse in the region; Lyle: the raise is generous, but reject the offer unless the short-notice overtime clause is removed.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Lyle grants Moreno’s point about the raise, so that’s not the fight. The fight is the bottom line: Moreno says accept the offer as it stands; Lyle says don’t, not with that clause in it. We need an answer about accepting the current offer.

choices.note: Tempting, since it’s Moreno’s main reason. But Lyle calls the raise ‘certainly generous’ and never challenges the comparison. No disagreement here.
Lyle says yes, but Moreno says nothing about child care. One speaker silent means no disagreement you can prove.
Too strong, and nobody says it. Moreno relies on the raise but never claims it’s the most important feature of every contract.
Neither speaker predicts what the company will do. Lyle only says what the union should do if the clause stays.
CORRECT. Moreno: accept it. Lyle: reject it unless the clause is removed, so not in its current form. Clear yes versus no.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Many of our older customers have trouble opening child-resistant medicine bottles, and some of them stop taking their medications as a result. Any customer can ask for easy-open caps instead, but few customers know this. So if we post signs at the counter announcing that easy-open caps are available on request, fewer of our older customers will stop taking their medications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the pharmacist’s argument?
choices: Most older customers who stop taking their medications do so because they cannot open the bottles.
Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy no more than child-resistant caps do.
Some older customers who have trouble opening child-resistant bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.
Older customers are more likely than younger customers to stop taking their prescribed medications.
Signs at the counter are the most effective way to inform customers that easy-open caps are available.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if the signs actually reach some of the customers who struggle with the caps and lead them to ask for easy-open ones; negate (C) and the signs change nothing. (A) is tempting, but the argument needs only some customers to be helped, not a majority of those who stop. (E) is too strong: the signs need to work, not to be the best method.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Posting signs about easy-open caps will lead fewer older customers to stop taking their medications.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some older customers stop taking medications because they can’t open child-resistant bottles; easy-open caps are available on request; few customers know this.

breakdown.analysis: So what if there’s a sign? A sign only helps if someone who needs it sees it and acts on it. If every struggling customer ignored the sign or never asked, nothing would change. We need an answer that says at least some of the right customers will notice and ask. Assumption answers are often modest like this: ‘some,’ not ‘most.’

choices.note: Tempting, because it makes the caps sound like the main problem. But the argument only needs some customers to be helped. Negate it: even if most quit for other reasons, the ones who quit because of caps could still be helped. No damage.
choices.negation: Not most older customers who stop taking their medications do so because they can’t open the bottles.

choices.note: Cost is a different dimension. Negate it: easy-open caps cost more. The signs could still keep customers on their medications. No damage.
choices.negation: Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy more than child-resistant caps do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the struggling customers would notice the signs and ask. Then the signs change nothing and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: No older customers who have trouble opening the bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.

choices.note: An irrelevant comparison. Negate it: older customers are no more likely to stop than younger ones. The plan can still help the older ones who do stop. No damage.
choices.negation: Older customers are not more likely than younger customers to stop taking their medications.

choices.note: Too strong. The signs only have to work, not be the best option. Negate it: some other method is more effective. The signs could still help. No damage.
choices.negation: Signs at the counter are not the most effective way to inform customers about easy-open caps.

questions.stimulus: Many residents of Corbin believe that the sinkholes that keep opening around town are caused by blasting at the quarry that opened four years ago. But sinkholes have opened in the Corbin area at about the same rate for the past hundred years, both before and since the quarry opened, and they are just as common on the far side of the valley, well beyond the reach of the blasting. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the quarry’s blasting is probably not what is causing Corbin’s sinkholes
the blasting at the quarry has made sinkholes in Corbin more frequent than they would otherwise be
sinkholes will stop opening in Corbin once the quarry closes
no human activity contributes to the formation of sinkholes
the bedrock beneath Corbin is dissolving faster now than it did a century ago
questions.explanation: The rate of sinkholes didn’t change when the quarry opened, and sinkholes are just as common where blasting can’t reach, so the evidence points away from the quarry as the cause; (A) completes the pushback. (B) repeats the popular view that the author is arguing against. (C) and (E) contradict the unchanged rate, and (D) is far broader than the evidence about one quarry.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Residents blame the quarry’s blasting for Corbin’s sinkholes; 2. sinkholes have opened at the same rate for a century, before and after the quarry opened; 3. they are just as common beyond the blasting’s reach.

breakdown.analysis: The word ‘But’ tells you the author is pushing back on the residents. If the quarry were the cause, you’d expect more sinkholes after it opened and more near it. Neither is true. So the blank should say the quarry probably isn’t the cause. Watch for the trap that repeats the popular view the author rejects.

choices.note: CORRECT. No change in the rate after the quarry opened and no difference outside the blasting zone: both facts point away from the quarry. ‘Probably’ fits the strength of the evidence.
Tempting if you read fast, because it’s what the residents believe. But the author says ‘But’ and gives evidence against exactly this. It’s the view being rejected.
Contradicts the evidence. Sinkholes opened at the same rate before the quarry existed, so there’s no reason to expect them to stop when it closes.
Too broad. The argument is about one quarry in one town. It says nothing about all human activity everywhere.
Contradicts the facts. The sinkhole rate is the same as a century ago, which gives no support for faster dissolving now.

questions.stimulus: Athletic director: At the start of last season, our high school required every player on its soccer teams to wear a newly designed padded headband. Over the season, team trainers recorded 30 percent fewer head injuries among our soccer players than in the season before. So the headbands made our players safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the athletic director’s argument?
choices: Players on the school’s basketball and lacrosse teams were not required to wear padded headbands last season.
Many of the soccer players complained throughout the season that the headbands were hot, heavy, and uncomfortable to wear.
In both seasons, the trainers recorded every head injury that occurred, no matter how minor.
Although fewer head injuries were recorded last season, more of them were serious concussions that sidelined players for weeks.
The headbands cost the school more than its athletic department had expected.
questions.explanation: The director measures safety by the number of head injuries, but if the injuries that did happen were more often severe concussions, the players may not be safer at all; (D) introduces severity. (C) is the trap: it shows the counts were recorded consistently, which if anything helps the argument. (A), (B), and (E) are about other teams, comfort, and cost, none of which bears on safety.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The headbands made the soccer players safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the headbands were required, trainers recorded 30 percent fewer head injuries.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of injuries really the measure of safety? Ten bumped heads can be less dangerous than three serious concussions. The director counts injuries but ignores how bad they are. We need an answer that shows the injuries got worse even as the count went down. This is a measure mismatch: counts versus severity.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Basketball players aren’t part of the argument. Right topic, wrong group.
Comfort is a different dimension. Uncomfortable headbands can still prevent injuries.
Tempting, because it’s about how the injuries were counted. But it says the counting was consistent across both seasons, which supports the comparison. It doesn’t weaken anything.
CORRECT. Fewer injuries, but more serious concussions. If the injuries that happen are worse, the drop in the count doesn’t show the players were safer.
Cost is a different dimension. The headbands can be expensive and still make players safer.

questions.stimulus: Planning commissioner: The city should grant a developer’s request to exceed a neighborhood’s height limit if the proposed building will include either affordable housing units or a new public park, provided that the proposal has first been presented at a public hearing held in that neighborhood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the planning commissioner?
choices: The Kell Tower proposal includes affordable housing units, and no hearing on it has been held yet, so the city should grant the developer’s request to exceed the height limit.
The Ardent Row proposal includes a new public park and was presented at a public hearing in its neighborhood, so the city should grant the request to exceed that neighborhood’s height limit.
The Lowe Street proposal was presented at a public hearing in its neighborhood, where residents spoke strongly in its favor, so the city should grant the request to exceed the height limit.

The Pardee proposal includes both affordable units and a public park but was presented only at a citywide hearing held downtown; nevertheless, the city should grant its request to exceed the height limit.
The Wilton proposal includes neither affordable units nor a public park, so the city should deny its request to exceed the height limit, even though it was presented at a hearing in its neighborhood.
questions.explanation: The principle says to grant the request when the building includes affordable units or a park and the proposal was presented at a hearing in that neighborhood; Ardent Row meets both conditions, (B). (E) is tempting, but the principle only says when to grant a request; it never says to deny one that falls short. (A) and (D) fail the neighborhood-hearing condition, and (C) fails the affordable-housing-or-park condition.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: (Affordable units OR new public park) AND presented at a hearing in that neighborhood → city should grant the height exception.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the project that meets both parts and gets the conclusion ‘grant.’

breakdown.analysis: Two conditions must both be met: (1) affordable housing or a park, either one is enough; (2) a hearing held in that neighborhood. Then the conclusion must be ‘grant.’ Note what the principle doesn’t say: nothing tells the city to deny a request. Traps will each satisfy only part of this.

choices.note: Condition 1 is met (affordable units), but there’s been no hearing. Condition 2 fails, so the principle doesn’t back granting.
CORRECT. A park satisfies the ‘either/or’ condition, and the hearing was held in the neighborhood. Both conditions met, and the judgment is ‘grant.’
Hearing in the neighborhood, yes, but there’s no affordable housing or park. Residents’ enthusiasm isn’t one of the conditions.
It has both features, but the hearing was citywide and downtown, not in the neighborhood. The principle requires a hearing ‘held in that neighborhood.’
Tempting, since Wilton really does fail condition 1. But the principle only tells you when to grant. Failing a sufficient condition doesn’t trigger a denial. That’s reversing the logic.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director at Pellbrook Press: Every novel on this year’s Coastal Booksellers bestseller list was promoted with a tour of podcast interviews. So if we arrange podcast tours for our debut novelists this spring, their novels will make that list.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the marketing director’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that podcast tours are more effective than other forms of book promotion
draws a conclusion about all novels from a sample consisting only of novels by debut authors
fails to consider that the Coastal Booksellers list might not accurately reflect sales
takes for granted that Pellbrook’s debut novelists would be willing to go on podcast tours
treats a feature shared by all the bestselling novels as enough to make a novel a bestseller
questions.explanation: Knowing that every bestseller had a podcast tour shows at most that such a tour goes along with making the list, not that a tour guarantees it; many toured novels may have missed the list. (E) names this necessary-versus-sufficient confusion. (A) is tempting, but the director never compares podcasts with other promotion. (D) is merely possible and wouldn’t fix the argument even if the novelists were eager.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Pellbrook gives its debut novelists podcast tours, their novels will make the bestseller list.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every novel on this year’s bestseller list had a podcast tour.

breakdown.analysis: Bestseller → podcast tour. The director flips it into podcast tour → bestseller. That’s confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one. Maybe hundreds of novels had podcast tours and sank without a trace. It’s like saying every Olympic sprinter wears running shoes, so if I buy running shoes I’ll make the Olympics. We need an answer that says the argument treats something all the winners share as a guarantee of winning.

choices.note: Tempting, because the director clearly loves podcasts. But there’s no comparison with other promotion anywhere. The argument would be just as flawed if podcasts were the best method.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Podcast tours sold some books last year, so they’re clearly the best way to promote any novel.

choices.note: Backwards. The evidence is about bestselling novels in general, and the conclusion is about debut novels, not the other way around.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The three debut novels we published did well, so every novel we publish will do well.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the list is unreliable, and the flaw remains even if the list is perfect.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our book topped the list, so it outsold everything else, even though the list counts only a few stores.

choices.note: Merely possible, and beside the point. Even if every novelist happily toured, a tour still wouldn’t guarantee a bestseller.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We’ll book our authors on a twenty-city tour, so they will certainly do all twenty events.

choices.note: CORRECT. All the bestsellers had tours, so a tour may be necessary, but the director treats it as sufficient. Lots of toured novels could have missed the list.

questions.stimulus: Every worker at the Sayer foundry who took an unpaid leave of more than two weeks last year had that leave approved by the shop steward. Last year the steward approved such leaves only for workers with at least three years of seniority, and she approved none that included any days in December. Ilse, who has worked at the foundry for five years, took an unpaid leave of three weeks last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The steward approved Ilse’s leave in some month other than December.
Every worker with at least three years of seniority who requested a leave outside December last year had the leave approved.
Any worker who took an unpaid leave of two weeks or less last year did so without the steward’s approval.
None of the days of Ilse’s leave last year fell in December.
Ilse’s leave was the longest unpaid leave taken by any foundry worker last year.
questions.explanation: Ilse’s three-week leave was longer than two weeks, so the steward approved it, and the steward approved no such leave that included December days, so Ilse’s leave had none; that is (D). (A) is the trap: the rule limits which leaves were approved, not when the approval was given. (B) reverses a necessary condition into a sufficient one, and (C) and (E) go beyond the facts.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Unpaid leave over two weeks last year → approved by steward; 2. approved → at least three years’ seniority; 3. approved → no December days; 4. Ilse took a three-week unpaid leave last year.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Ilse’s leave was over two weeks → approved by the steward → no December days (and Ilse has the seniority, which we already knew). So we can prove her leave had no December days. Watch for answers that reverse a link or quietly change what the rule is about.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the December rule. But the rule is about leaves that include December days, not about when the steward signed off. She could have approved Ilse’s June leave in December.
This reverses the seniority rule. Seniority is necessary for approval, not a guarantee of it.
We don’t know this. The facts only cover leaves longer than two weeks. Shorter leaves might also need approval; we’re told nothing about them.
CORRECT. Over two weeks → approved → no December days. Ilse’s leave fits the chain, so none of it fell in December.
Unsupported ranking. Nothing tells us how long anyone else’s leave was.

questions.stimulus: Preservationist: Councilor Brandt proposes protecting from demolition every building in Oakhurst that is more than fifty years old, on the grounds that age alone gives a building historic value. But under that standard, the cinder-block bus garage put up on Mercer Road in 1968 would merit the same protection as the town’s colonial courthouse. No one seriously regards that garage as a landmark. So age alone cannot be what gives a building historic value.
questions.stem: The claim that the bus garage would merit the same protection as the colonial courthouse plays which one of the following roles in the preservationist’s argument?
choices: It is presented as a consequence of Councilor Brandt’s standard that the preservationist takes to be unacceptable.
It is the conclusion that the preservationist’s argument is designed to establish.
It is a premise that Councilor Brandt offers in support of the proposal.
It is offered as evidence that the courthouse has less historic value than is commonly believed.
It is a claim that the preservationist accepts and uses to show that some old buildings deserve protection.
questions.explanation: The preservationist derives the garage claim from Brandt’s age-only standard and then treats it as absurd, since no one considers the garage a landmark, in order to reject the standard; (A) describes this. (E) is the trap: the preservationist does not believe the garage deserves protection. (B) is wrong because the conclusion is that age alone can’t confer historic value, and (C) is wrong because Brandt never mentions the garage.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Age alone cannot be what gives a building historic value.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brandt’s age-only standard would protect a 1968 cinder-block bus garage just like the colonial courthouse; no one thinks the garage is a landmark.

breakdown.analysis: This is a ‘reduce it to absurdity’ move. The preservationist says: follow Brandt’s rule and you get a ridiculous result, the garage gets courthouse-level protection. The author doesn’t believe this. It’s the absurd result used to sink the rule. We need an answer that calls the claim an unacceptable consequence of Brandt’s standard.

choices.note: CORRECT. The garage claim follows from Brandt’s standard, and the preservationist finds it unacceptable. That’s what knocks out the standard.
The conclusion is the last sentence: age alone can’t give historic value. The garage claim supports that; it isn’t it.
Brandt never mentions the garage. The preservationist is the one who brings it up, against Brandt.
Nothing knocks the courthouse. The courthouse is the obvious landmark the garage is compared to.

Tempting, because the preservationist does state the claim. But the preservationist rejects it: ‘No one seriously regards that garage as a landmark.’ It’s used to sink the standard, not to protect old buildings.

questions.stimulus: Publisher: Our press built its reputation on accuracy, and we should not put that reputation at risk. Dr. Ames’s history of Harrow Lake makes many claims about local families that no one has checked against public records. So we should not publish the book in its current form.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the publisher’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Publishing a book that contains factual errors would put the press’s reputation for accuracy at risk.
Most histories of small communities contain at least some errors about local families.
The press should not publish a book containing claims about local families unless those claims have been checked against public records.
Any book whose claims about local families have been checked against public records is accurate enough for the press to publish.
Dr. Ames did not consult any public records while writing his history of Harrow Lake.
questions.explanation: The book contains claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records; if checking such claims is required before publishing, the book can’t be published as is, so (C) guarantees the conclusion. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient-condition version, telling us when a book may be published, which says nothing about an unchecked one. (A) fails because unchecked claims aren’t shown to be errors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The press should not publish Ames’s book in its current form.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The press shouldn’t risk its reputation for accuracy; the book has many claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records.

breakdown.analysis: Unchecked isn’t the same as wrong. So how do we get from ‘unchecked claims’ to ‘don’t publish’? The cleanest bridge makes checking a requirement: publish → claims checked. The book’s claims weren’t checked, so by the contrapositive: not checked → don’t publish. Chain: book has unchecked family claims → (rule) → should not publish. Watch for the sufficient version of this rule; it points the wrong way.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties into the reputation premise. But the book’s claims are unchecked, not shown to be false. Without knowing there are errors, this rule never kicks in.
‘Most histories’ having some errors makes errors likely, not certain, and still doesn’t say errors mean don’t publish. Not enough to force the conclusion.
CORRECT. Checking against public records is now a requirement for publication. The book fails it, so it shouldn’t be published as is.

Tempting, but it’s the wrong direction. It says when checked books may be published. It says nothing about what to do with an unchecked one. It’s the sufficient version of the needed necessary condition.
This explains why the claims are unchecked, which we already know. It still doesn’t tell us that unchecked means don’t publish.

questions.stimulus: In surveys, patients in the Calloway health system named cost more often than any other reason for failing to refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time. Yet after Calloway made its most widely prescribed blood-pressure drug free to its patients, the proportion of patients taking that drug who failed to refill it on time did not decline at all.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why making the drug free did not reduce the proportion of late refills?
choices: Fewer than half of the patients who reported failing to refill on time named cost as their main reason for doing so.
Most patients collect all their prescriptions in one pharmacy visit, and those short of money delay that visit because their other drugs are not free.
Patients who refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time suffer fewer strokes than patients who do not.
The free drug is as effective as the more expensive blood-pressure drugs that Calloway’s physicians sometimes prescribe.
Some patients fail to refill their prescriptions on time simply because they lose track of when a refill is due.
questions.explanation: If patients collect all their prescriptions in one visit and short-of-money patients put off that whole visit because of the other, still-costly drugs, then the free drug gets refilled late anyway, so cost still drives the delay; that is (B). (A) and (E) are tempting because they point to reasons other than cost, but as long as cost was the most common reason, removing it should have reduced late refills at least somewhat, and the puzzle is that they didn’t decline at all.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cost was the top reason for late refills, but making the drug free didn’t reduce late refills of it at all.

breakdown.analysis: If cost is the main reason people refill late, why didn’t ‘free’ help even a little? Maybe the cost that matters isn’t this drug’s price. If patients buy everything in one trip, and the trip is still expensive because of the other drugs, then making one drug free doesn’t change when they show up. We need an answer that shows cost still blocks the refill even though this drug is free.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shrinks the cost group. But cost was still the most common reason. Removing it should have reduced late refills somewhat, and they didn’t decline at all.

CORRECT. The refill is tied to one pharmacy trip, and that trip still costs money because of the other drugs. Patients short of cash postpone the whole trip, so the free drug is refilled late just as before. Cost still explains the delay.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. It tells us why refilling on time matters, not why the free drug didn’t change behavior.
Effectiveness is a different dimension. It doesn’t explain anything about refill timing.
Tempting, since forgetting is another cause. But ‘some’ forget doesn’t explain why the cost group, the biggest group, didn’t improve.

questions.stimulus: City planner: Ten years ago, Wexley ranked third among the region’s twelve cities in the percentage of commuters who travel to work by bicycle. This year it ranked seventh. Clearly, the money Wexley spent on bike lanes during the past decade did not prevent bicycle commuting in Wexley from declining.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the city planner’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that bike lanes might provide benefits other than an increase in bicycle commuting
overlooks the possibility that bicycle commuting in Wexley would have fallen even further without the new bike lanes
presumes, without providing justification, that the region’s other cities spent less on bike lanes than Wexley did
ignores the possibility that Wexley’s population grew more slowly over the decade than the populations of other cities in the region
takes for granted that because Wexley fell in the ranking, the percentage of its commuters who bike must have fallen
questions.explanation: Dropping from third to seventh shows only that other cities now outrank Wexley; Wexley’s own bicycle share could have stayed level or risen while several other cities rose faster, so (E) names the flaw. (B) is the strongest trap, but the conclusion is only that the spending did not prevent a decline; if a decline happened, that is true even if things would have been worse without the lanes. (D) is irrelevant because the ranking is by percentage, which already adjusts for population.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bike-lane spending didn’t prevent bicycle commuting in Wexley from declining.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wexley fell from third to seventh in the region in percentage of commuters who bike.

breakdown.analysis: Did biking in Wexley actually go down? All we know is its rank dropped. Rankings are relative. Picture it: Wexley went from 8 percent to 10 percent, but four other cities jumped from 6 to 12. Wexley slides to seventh while its biking grows. Moving down a ranking isn’t an absolute decrease; that’s a classic trap, know it. We need an answer that says the planner treats a lower rank as a lower percentage.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is only about whether biking declined, not whether the lanes were worthwhile overall.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The bike lanes didn’t raise cycling, so they were a total waste of money.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the classic ‘it could have been worse’ objection. But the conclusion only says the spending didn’t prevent a decline. If biking declined, that’s true even if it would have fallen further without the lanes. The real problem is that we don’t know there was any decline.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since we hired more police, crime rose 5 percent, so the hiring increased crime, even though crime might have risen 20 percent without it.

choices.note: The planner doesn’t compare spending among cities at all. Nothing in the argument depends on what others spent.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Wexley outspent everyone on bike lanes, so it must have the most cyclists.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The ranking is by percentage of commuters, which already adjusts for population size. Population growth doesn’t affect it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Wexley has more cyclists than Tull, so a larger share of Wexley’s commuters must bike.

choices.note: CORRECT. A drop in rank shows only that other cities passed Wexley. Wexley’s own percentage could have held steady or even risen.

questions.stimulus: Food writer: Some cooking instructors define a braise as any dish in which meat is cooked slowly in liquid in a covered pot. But consider a whole chicken poached gently in a covered pot of simmering stock. It satisfies this definition, yet no experienced cook would call it a braise. So the instructors’ definition is too broad.
questions.stem: The food writer’s argument proceeds by
choices: presenting a case that meets a proposed definition but to which the term being defined does not apply
presenting a case to which the term being defined applies but that a proposed definition fails to include
arguing that a definition is unreliable because those who proposed it lack relevant experience
showing that two competing definitions of a term classify the same dish in contradictory ways
inferring that because one dish cooked in liquid is not a braise, no dish cooked in liquid is a braise
questions.explanation: The poached chicken fits the instructors’ definition (meat, slow cooking, liquid, covered pot) but isn’t a braise, so the definition lets in something it should exclude, which is what (A) describes. (B) is the reverse: it describes showing a definition is too narrow, not too broad. (C) misreads the appeal to experienced cooks, which is about how the term is used, not about the instructors’ qualifications.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The instructors’ definition of a braise is too broad.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Poached chicken fits the definition, but no experienced cook would call it a braise.

breakdown.analysis: The move is a counterexample to a definition. Which kind? A definition can fail two ways: too broad (it lets in things that don’t belong) or too narrow (it leaves out things that do). Poached chicken fits the definition but isn’t a braise, so it gets in when it shouldn’t. That’s too broad. We need an answer that says ‘a case that meets the definition but isn’t the thing.’

choices.note: CORRECT. The poached chicken meets every part of the definition, yet it isn’t a braise. That’s exactly how you show a definition is too broad.
Tempting, because it’s also a counterexample to a definition. But it’s the too-narrow kind: a real braise the definition leaves out. Here the chicken is inside the definition and isn’t a braise.
choices.example: Example of this method: Some define a braise as meat cooked in wine. But short ribs braised in beer are clearly a braise, so the definition is too narrow.

choices.note: The writer never attacks the instructors’ experience. ‘No experienced cook would call it a braise’ is about how the word is used, not about the instructors.
choices.example: Example of this method: These instructors have never worked in a restaurant, so their definition of a braise can’t be trusted.

choices.note: Only one definition is on the table. The writer never offers a competing one.
choices.example: Example of this method: One chef defines a stew by its liquid and another by its cut of meat, and the two definitions disagree about chili.

choices.note: The writer doesn’t generalize from one dish. The point is that this one dish shows the definition fails, not that nothing cooked in liquid is a braise.
choices.example: Example of this method: Poached chicken isn’t a braise, so pot roast and short ribs aren’t either.

questions.stimulus: Labor historian: In 1987 the sawmills of the Brisco Valley cut their workers’ wages by 15 percent. Over the next two years, nearly a third of the mills’ experienced workers left for jobs elsewhere, and the mills’ output fell sharply. Clearly, the wage cut was responsible for the mills’ loss of experienced workers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the labor historian’s argument?
choices: Most of the experienced workers who left the mills took jobs that paid more than the mills had paid before the wage cut.
The sharp fall in the mills’ output was caused mainly by the departure of experienced workers.
No experienced workers had left the mills during the years before the wage cut.
Many of the experienced workers who left the mills in those two years would not have left had their wages not been cut.
The wage cut at the Brisco Valley mills was larger than any wage cut made by other employers in the region at that time.
questions.explanation: To blame the departures on the wage cut, the historian must assume they would not have happened anyway; if nearly all those workers would have left even without the cut, the cut wasn’t responsible, so (D) is required. (C) is the most tempting trap, but it is too strong: some workers could have left before the cut and the cut could still explain the later wave. (B) concerns output, which the conclusion doesn’t address, and (A) requires ‘most,’ which goes beyond what the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The wage cut caused the mills’ loss of experienced workers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wages were cut 15 percent in 1987; over the next two years nearly a third of experienced workers left and output fell.

breakdown.analysis: Would those workers have left anyway? Maybe a big new employer opened nearby, or the mills were rumored to be closing. To blame the wage cut, the historian needs the departures not to have happened without it. That’s a counterfactual cause: blaming X requires that the outcome wouldn’t have happened without X. We need an answer saying many of those workers would have stayed if wages hadn’t been cut.

choices.note: Too strong. Negate it: not most found better-paying jobs. Workers could still have left because of the cut, say for jobs that paid more than the reduced wage. Not required.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the workers who left took jobs paying more than the pre-cut wage.

choices.note: Output is a side issue. The conclusion is only about losing workers. Negate it: output fell mainly for some other reason. The wage cut could still explain the departures. Not required.
choices.negation: The fall in output was not caused mainly by the departure of experienced workers.

choices.note: Tempting, because a steady drip of departures before the cut would complicate things. But it’s too strong. Negate it: a few workers had left before. The cut can still explain the big wave afterward. Not required.
choices.negation: Some experienced workers had left the mills during the years before the wage cut.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: few if any of those workers would have stayed without the cut; they’d have left anyway. Then the cut wasn’t responsible, and the conclusion falls apart.
choices.negation: Few, if any, of the workers who left would have stayed had their wages not been cut.

choices.note: An irrelevant comparison. Negate it: other employers cut wages just as much. The Brisco cut could still be why these workers left. Not required.
choices.negation: The Brisco Valley wage cut was not larger than every other regional employer’s wage cut.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacy manager: Every prescription our pharmacy fills for a controlled substance is recorded in the state monitoring database. The prescription Mr. Okafor picked up yesterday appears in that database. So it must have been for a controlled substance.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the pharmacy manager’s argument is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: A bus may enter the downtown transit mall only if it carries a city permit. The bus now parked at the depot carries no city permit, so it may not enter the downtown transit mall.
A cake at Pella’s Café is labeled gluten-free only if it was baked on a Tuesday, after the ovens are cleaned. This torte was baked on a Tuesday, so it must be labeled gluten-free.
Every student who passed the final exam received a certificate. Mira did not pass the final exam, so she must not have received a certificate.
Most of the tenants who signed the petition attended the building meeting. Hal attended the building meeting, so he probably signed the petition.
Every member of the choir sings at the spring festival, and everyone who sings at the festival receives a free ticket. So every member of the choir receives a free ticket.
questions.explanation: The manager reasons: controlled substance → recorded; Okafor’s prescription was recorded; so it was a controlled substance, mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one. (B) has the same form once its ‘only if’ is translated: labeled gluten-free → baked Tuesday; the torte was baked Tuesday; so it’s labeled gluten-free. (D) is the strongest trap, but it uses ‘most’ and ‘probably,’ a different and weaker pattern; (A) and (E) are valid, and (C) negates the condition rather than affirming the result.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mr. Okafor’s prescription was for a controlled substance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every controlled-substance prescription is recorded in the database; Okafor’s prescription is recorded.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; this thing is B; so it is A. (Affirming the result of a conditional.)

breakdown.analysis: Controlled → recorded. Recorded doesn’t mean controlled; maybe the pharmacy records lots of other prescriptions too. It’s like saying every dog has four legs, my cat has four legs, so my cat is a dog. Now find the same error: a rule A → B, a case with B, a conclusion of A. Careful: ‘only if’ introduces the necessary condition, so ‘X only if Y’ means X → Y. Translate every choice before matching.

choices.note: Tempting on the surface because of the ‘only if.’ Translate it: enter → permit. No permit → can’t enter. That’s the contrapositive, which is valid. Our stimulus is flawed, so this doesn’t match.

CORRECT. Labeled gluten-free → baked Tuesday. The torte was baked Tuesday, so it must be labeled gluten-free. Same mistake: having the necessary condition is treated as proof of the other. The ‘only if’ wording hides the match.
A different flaw. Passed → certificate. Mira didn’t pass, so no certificate. That’s negating the first part, not affirming the second. She could have earned a certificate some other way.

Tempting, because it runs in the same backward direction. But it starts from ‘most’ and ends with ‘probably,’ a probabilistic argument. The stimulus uses ‘every’ and ‘must.’ Close, but not the same pattern.
Valid. Choir → sings → ticket, so choir → ticket. A clean chain, no flaw, so it can’t match a flawed argument.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: Three years ago, Corvale planted shade trees along the length of Bram Street. Since then, the number of pedestrians using Bram Street on summer afternoons has risen by a quarter. Evidently, the shade has made walking on Bram Street more appealing in hot weather.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the urban planner’s argument?
choices: Several new shops and cafés have opened on Bram Street during the past three years.
On nearby Tull Street, which has no shade trees, pedestrian counts on summer afternoons have also risen by about a quarter in three years.
Shade trees lower sidewalk temperatures more in dry climates than they do in humid ones.
Planting the trees along Bram Street cost the city less than its planners had projected.
Bram Street’s pedestrian counts on summer mornings and winter afternoons, when shade matters little, have not risen in three years.
questions.explanation: If pedestrian traffic rose only at the times when shade matters, a general increase in foot traffic (new shops, population growth) becomes an unlikely explanation and the shade becomes the likely cause; (E) does this. (C) is tempting because it says shade cools sidewalks, but it doesn’t tell us what kind of climate Corvale has or that cooler sidewalks drew more walkers. (A) and (B) point to other causes and so weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The shade trees made walking on Bram Street more appealing in hot weather.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the trees were planted, summer-afternoon pedestrian counts on Bram Street rose by a quarter.

breakdown.analysis: Maybe Bram Street just got busier for other reasons: new businesses, more residents, a new bus stop. How do we know it’s the shade? A great test: look at times when shade doesn’t matter. If traffic rose only on hot afternoons, the shade looks like the cause. If it rose all the time, something else is going on. We need an answer that shows the increase lines up with when shade matters.

choices.note: Alternative cause. New shops could explain more pedestrians at every hour. That weakens.
Weakens. A similar street with no trees saw the same jump, so something citywide, not the shade, is likely driving the increase.

Tempting, because it says shade cools sidewalks. But we don’t know Corvale’s climate, and cooler sidewalks don’t by themselves show that people walked there more because of it. Too vague to help much.
Cost is a different dimension. It says nothing about why pedestrians came.
CORRECT. Traffic rose only when shade matters (summer afternoons) and stayed flat at times when shade doesn’t matter. That rules out a general rise in foot traffic and points to the shade.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: The mineral marlite forms only where molten volcanic rock comes into contact with seawater. Once exposed to air, marlite breaks down completely within two thousand years. Last year a landslide in the Corrin Highlands, far from any present-day coast, sheared away the face of a cliff, and the newly exposed rock contains abundant marlite.
questions.stem: The geologist’s statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The marlite in the Corrin Highlands cliff must have formed sometime within the last two thousand years.
Any rock in the Corrin Highlands that has been exposed to air for several centuries contains no marlite.
The rock containing the cliff’s marlite has never, since the marlite formed, been exposed to air for two thousand years or more.
Most of the marlite that has formed anywhere on Earth has since broken down completely as a result of exposure to air.
Marlite is more abundant in the Corrin Highlands than in rock near present-day coasts.
questions.explanation: If the marlite-bearing rock had ever been exposed to air for two thousand years or more, the marlite would have broken down completely; since the rock still contains abundant marlite, it was never exposed that long, which is (C). (A) is the main trap: the breakdown clock runs only while the rock is exposed to air, so buried marlite could be millions of years old. (B) misreads the time scale, since centuries are less than two thousand years.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Marlite forms only where molten volcanic rock meets seawater; 2. exposed to air, marlite breaks down completely within 2,000 years; 3. last year’s landslide exposed cliff rock in the inland Corrin Highlands containing abundant marlite.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to predict exactly, but fact 2 is a clock, and it only ticks while marlite is exposed to air. Exposed for 2,000+ years → no marlite left. Contrapositive: marlite still there → never exposed that long. The cliff rock still has plenty of marlite, so it was never exposed for 2,000 years. Watch for answers that treat the clock as running from when the marlite formed, or that stretch the time scale.

choices.note: Tempting, because ‘two thousand years’ matches the clock. But the clock only runs while the marlite is exposed to air. Rock sealed inside a cliff could hold marlite that formed millions of years ago.
Wrong time scale. Breakdown is complete within 2,000 years, but after only a few centuries some marlite could remain. ‘Contains no marlite’ goes too far.
CORRECT. Exposure of 2,000+ years would leave no marlite. This rock has abundant marlite, so it was never exposed that long. That follows directly from the facts.
We don’t know this. The facts say nothing about how much marlite has ever formed or how much has been exposed.
Unsupported comparison. We’re told nothing about how much marlite exists near coasts.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: A prescription for a drug in the restricted category can be refilled without a new consultation only if the prescribing physician has signed a long-term-use authorization for that patient within the past year. Dr. Hale, who prescribes Velacor for Mr. Ruiz, signs such authorizations only during in-person examinations, and she has not examined Mr. Ruiz in person in more than two years. So Velacor must not be in the restricted category.
questions.stem: The pharmacist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Mr. Ruiz’s prescription for Velacor was refilled last week without a new consultation.
Dr. Hale has not signed a long-term-use authorization for Mr. Ruiz within the past year.
Any drug whose prescriptions can be refilled without a new consultation is outside the restricted category.
If Dr. Hale had examined Mr. Ruiz in person within the past year, she would have signed a long-term-use authorization for his Velacor prescription.
Some of Dr. Hale’s other patients have had their Velacor prescriptions refilled without a new consultation.
questions.explanation: Hale signs authorizations only during in-person exams and hasn’t examined Ruiz in two years, so Ruiz has no authorization from the past year; if Velacor were restricted, his prescription therefore couldn’t be refilled without a consultation. If it was in fact refilled last week without one, Velacor can’t be restricted, so (A) completes the proof. (B) is tempting but only restates what the premises already establish, and (E) fails because other patients may have recent authorizations.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velacor is not in the restricted category.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Restricted drug refilled without consultation → prescriber signed an authorization for that patient within the past year; Hale signs only during in-person exams; Hale hasn’t examined Ruiz in over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain. Hale signs only at exams + no exam in two years → no authorization for Ruiz in the past year. Rule: restricted AND refilled without consultation → authorization in past year. Contrapositive: no authorization → NOT (restricted AND refilled without consultation). So for Ruiz, either Velacor isn’t restricted or his prescription wasn’t refilled without a consultation. To force ‘not restricted,’ we need the missing fact: Ruiz’s Velacor was refilled without a consultation. Here the answer is a plain fact, not a rule, which makes it easy to skip.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ruiz got a refill without a consultation (last week, well within the window) and had no authorization from the past year. If Velacor were restricted, that refill couldn’t have happened. So Velacor isn’t restricted.
Tempting, because it’s a real step in the chain. But the premises already prove it. Adding it gives nothing new; we still don’t know whether Ruiz ever got a refill without a consultation.

This is about drugs that can be refilled without consultation, but nothing says Velacor can be for Ruiz. And restricted drugs can be refilled without a consultation when an authorization exists, so this rule doesn’t fit the stimulus anyway.
A sufficient-condition trap. It tells us what Hale would have done after an exam, but there was no exam, so it tells us nothing new. It doesn’t connect to whether Velacor is restricted.
Wrong group. Other patients may have been examined recently and have valid authorizations. Their refills prove nothing about Velacor’s category.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Adult male Tolland warblers have a white patch on the tail that is visible only when the tail is spread. Males spread their tails far more often during the three weeks before pairs form than at any other time of year. So the patch most likely serves to attract mates.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ornithologist’s argument?
choices: Females of a closely related warbler species prefer to pair with males whose tail patches are larger than average.
The tail patch is slightly larger and brighter on older males than it is on younger ones.
Many songbird species have markings that are visible only when the birds spread their wings or tails in flight.
After pairs have formed for the season, male Tolland warblers seldom spread their tails at all.
Migrating hawks pass through in the weeks before pairs form, and males spread their tails mostly when a hawk is in view.
questions.explanation: The argument infers the patch’s function from when it is displayed; (E) shows the timing is explained by hawks passing through and that males flash the patch in response to hawks, suggesting an alarm or predator-deterrent function instead. (D) is the trap: it fits the mate-attraction story by showing displays drop after pairing, so it strengthens rather than weakens. (A) concerns a different species and, if anything, supports the ornithologist.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The male warbler’s tail patch most likely serves to attract mates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The patch shows only when the tail is spread; males spread their tails most in the three weeks before pairs form.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the displays peak before pairing? Lots of things could happen during those three weeks. The argument guesses a function from timing alone. The best weakener gives the patch a different job that explains the same timing. We need an answer that offers an alternative function, especially one that fits the three-week peak.

choices.note: Strengthens, if anything, by analogy: in a related species, the patch matters to females. Wrong direction.
Neutral. Bigger patches on older males fit either a mating or a non-mating function.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. That other birds have flight-only markings tells us nothing about what this patch does.
Tempting, because it’s about tail-spreading timing. But fewer displays after pairing fits the mate-attraction story. It strengthens.
CORRECT. The pre-pairing peak is explained by hawks passing through, and males flash the patch when a hawk appears. That points to a predator-related function and undercuts the mating inference.

questions.stimulus: Most of the recipes in Ilsa Ferro’s new cookbook require a stand mixer. Any recipe that requires a stand mixer is impractical for the many readers who cook in small apartment kitchens. So most of the recipes in Ferro’s cookbook are impractical for those readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every apartment in the Larch Building faces west, and most west-facing apartments in the city are hard to rent in summer. So most apartments in the Larch Building are hard to rent in summer.
Most apartments in the Larch Building will be hard to rent this summer, since most of them face west, and every west-facing apartment in the building is hard to rent in summer.
Most of the trails in Dunn Park are steep, and most of the steep trails in the park are closed in winter. So most of the trails in Dunn Park are closed in winter.
Most of the trucks in the Kell fleet run on diesel, and every diesel truck must be inspected yearly. So every truck in the Kell fleet that must be inspected yearly runs on diesel.
Every recipe in the cookbook that uses saffron is expensive to prepare, and most of the cookbook’s recipes are expensive to prepare. So most of the cookbook’s recipes use saffron.
questions.explanation: The argument has the valid form: most A are B; every B is C; so most A are C. (B) matches exactly (most apartments are west-facing; every west-facing one is hard to rent; so most are hard to rent), with the conclusion stated first. (C) is tempting but chains two ‘most’ statements, which doesn’t guarantee overlap; (A) reverses which statement uses ‘every,’ and (E) borrows the cookbook topic but reasons backward.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most recipes in Ferro’s cookbook are impractical for small-kitchen readers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most recipes need a stand mixer; every stand-mixer recipe is impractical for those readers.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; every B is C; so most A are C. (Valid.)

breakdown.analysis: This one is valid: if most recipes are in the ‘needs a mixer’ group, and everyone in that group is impractical, then most recipes are impractical. Now find the same shape: ‘most’ first, then an ‘every’ that covers the whole middle group, then ‘most’ in the conclusion. Don’t be thrown by an answer that puts its conclusion first, and don’t be lured by an answer that shares the cookbook topic.

choices.note: The quantifiers are swapped: every A is B, most B are C. The ‘most’ west-facing apartments that are hard to rent could all be in other buildings. Invalid, and a different pattern.

CORRECT. Most Larch apartments face west (most A are B); every west-facing Larch apartment is hard to rent (every B is C); so most Larch apartments are hard to rent (most A are C). The conclusion comes first, but the structure is identical.
Tempting, because it looks almost the same. But it’s most + most. The steep trails that are closed could be a small slice of all trails. Two ‘mosts’ don’t chain.
The conclusion reverses the ‘every’ statement: from ‘diesel → inspected’ it concludes ‘inspected → diesel.’ Different pattern, and invalid.
Same topic as the stimulus, which is the lure. But it’s backward: every saffron recipe is expensive and most recipes are expensive, so most use saffron. That reverses the conditional.

questions.stimulus: Labor mediator: The Oriel Hotel’s management wants to require its housekeepers to wear location-tracking badges throughout their shifts, saying the data would help it schedule cleaning more efficiently. But the same scheduling gains could be achieved by having housekeepers log each room as they finish it, which would reveal far less about their movements. So the hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the labor mediator’s argument?
choices: Before adopting a practice that affects how employees do their jobs, an employer should consult the employees affected.
An employer should adopt any practice that makes scheduling more efficient unless employees formally object to it.
If a workplace practice would make operations more efficient without intruding on employees’ privacy, an employer should adopt it.
An employer should not adopt a practice that intrudes on employees’ privacy if a less intrusive practice would serve the employer’s purpose equally well.
An employer should adopt a less intrusive practice in place of a more intrusive one only if the less intrusive practice also costs less.
questions.explanation: The mediator rejects the badges because room logging would achieve the same scheduling gains with less intrusion; (D) says exactly that an intrusive practice shouldn’t be adopted when a less intrusive one serves the purpose equally well. (C) is tempting but only supports adopting the logging system; it says nothing about rejecting the badges. (A) and (B) turn on consultation and objections, which the argument never mentions, and (E) adds a cost condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Room logging would give the same scheduling gains while revealing far less about housekeepers’ movements.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is ‘don’t adopt the badges.’ The reason is ‘a less intrusive option works just as well.’ So we need: if a less intrusive option serves the purpose equally well, don’t adopt the more intrusive one.

choices.note: Consultation never comes up. Even if the hotel consulted everyone, this principle wouldn’t say to reject the badges.
This would push toward adopting the badges unless someone objects, and no objection is mentioned. Wrong direction.
Tempting, because it praises the logging option. But it only says to adopt efficient, non-intrusive practices. It doesn’t tell you to reject the badges, which is the conclusion.
CORRECT. Badges intrude; logging is less intrusive and serves the purpose equally well; so don’t adopt the badges. Every piece matches.
Cost is a different dimension, and the argument says nothing about cost. This adds a condition we can’t check.

questions.stimulus: Literary agent: Admittedly, collections of previously published short stories rarely sell as well as novels do. But each of the twelve stories in Dara Vell’s new collection was praised by reviewers when it first appeared in a magazine. So reviewers will surely praise the collection as a whole.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the literary agent’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on the judgments of reviewers who may have been biased in the author’s favor
treats the fact that the stories were published in magazines as evidence that they are of high quality
presumes that because each part of a work has a certain quality, the whole work has it too
confuses praise from reviewers with success in the market for books
fails to consider that some of the stories in the collection may never have appeared in a magazine
questions.explanation: A collection of individually strong stories can still disappoint as a whole, for example if the stories feel repetitive side by side, so moving from ‘each story was praised’ to ‘the collection will be praised’ is a part-to-whole error, (C). (D) is tempting because of the concession about sales, but the agent sets sales aside and draws a conclusion only about reviewers’ praise. (E) contradicts the premise that each of the twelve stories appeared in a magazine.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reviewers will surely praise Vell’s collection as a whole.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of the collection’s twelve stories was praised when it first appeared in a magazine. (The agent concedes such collections rarely sell as well as novels.)

breakdown.analysis: So what if every story was praised on its own? A whole can be different from its parts. Twelve great stories might feel repetitive read back to back. It’s like saying every player on the team is an all-star, so the team will surely win the title. That’s the part-to-whole flaw (composition); it’s a classic, know it. The ‘admittedly’ sentence about sales is a side point the agent sets aside.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the reviewers were biased, and even unbiased praise of each story wouldn’t guarantee praise of the whole.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The reviewers loved her stories, and they’re all her old friends, so their praise proves the stories are excellent.

choices.note: The agent relies on reviewers’ praise, not on the mere fact of magazine publication. This describes evidence the argument doesn’t use.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Her stories ran in national magazines, so they must be excellent.

choices.note: CORRECT. Praise for each story is treated as a guarantee of praise for the collection. The parts having a quality doesn’t mean the whole has it.
Tempting, because the concession talks about sales. But the agent puts sales aside (‘Admittedly … But’) and concludes only about reviewers’ praise. No confusion between the two.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Critics adored the novel, so it will certainly be a bestseller.

choices.note: Contradicts the premise. The agent says each of the twelve stories appeared in a magazine, so there’s nothing to overlook.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The stories I know about were praised, so every story in the book was praised, though some may be new.

passages.title: Apology statutes
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Over the past few decades, many jurisdictions have adopted apology statutes, which prevent a person’s expression of sympathy after an accident or injury from being introduced as evidence of liability in a later lawsuit. Their rationale is straightforward: people, and physicians in particular, would apologize more readily if they did not fear that their words would be used against them, and injured parties who receive apologies would be less inclined to sue. Yet the statutes rest on uncertain ground.

First, most of them protect only expressions of sympathy (“I am sorry this happened to you”) while leaving admissions of fault fully admissible. They thus encourage precisely the kind of apology that injured people find least satisfying: one that acknowledges suffering but sidesteps responsibility. Such a gesture gives injured people little of what they actually seek.

Second, the statutes assume that fear of litigation is what keeps people from apologizing. But when the legal scholar Teodor Halvik asked hospital physicians why they had not apologized after a medical error, they cited embarrassment, uncertainty about what had gone wrong, and institutional habit at least as often as legal exposure. A rule of evidence can do nothing about these.

Third, and most troubling, the statutes invite strategic use. An insurer that coaches its policyholders to offer carefully worded, legally weightless expressions of regret may thereby defuse claims that deserve to be pursued. What was meant to make room for moral repair becomes one more instrument for managing liability.

Passage B

Critics of laws that shield apologies from use as evidence sometimes treat any apology made under such protection as suspect, as if an expression of regret could be sincere only when it is costly. But sincerity is not measured by legal risk. A driver who says “I’m so sorry” at the scene of a collision may mean it entirely, whether or not the words could later be read to a jury.

It is true that a protected statement of sympathy is not a confession of fault, and some injured people want the latter. But for many, what matters first is acknowledgment: evidence that the other party recognizes the harm done. In a study by Mirela Castan of mediated disputes over minor injuries, claimants who received an expression of sympathy were more willing to accept settlement offers than those who received none, even though the sympathy carried no admission of fault.

Nor need such laws work alone to be worthwhile. If people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one of those reasons still helps; no one argues that a seatbelt law is pointless because seatbelts do not prevent every traffic death.

Finally, the protection does what rules of evidence often do: it keeps out statements whose value as proof is small relative to the prejudice they create. Jurors tend to hear “I’m sorry” as “It was my fault,” though people routinely apologize for harms they did not cause. Excluding such statements makes verdicts more accurate, not less.

passages.title: Crab cues and periwinkle shells
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Along the coast of the Varn Peninsula, the banded periwinkle, a small grazing sea snail, differs strikingly between two neighboring bays.
