Periwinkles in Hesk Sound have shells nearly twice as thick as those of periwinkles in Tolley Inlet, only forty kilometers away. Because the snail’s larvae drift for weeks in coastal currents before settling, the two populations interbreed freely, and genetic surveys have found no differences between them. For years the contrast was attributed to the physical environment: Hesk Sound is more exposed to storm waves, and thicker shells were assumed to withstand being battered against rock.

The marine biologist Ruth Ambler doubted this account. Within Hesk Sound itself, she noted, periwinkles in sheltered coves have shells as thick as those on exposed headlands. What distinguishes the sound from the inlet, she observed, is not wave exposure but a predator: a shell-crushing crab that has been common in Hesk Sound for decades but has never become established in Tolley Inlet. Ambler proposed that shell thickness is not fixed at birth but is adjusted by each snail as it grows, in response to chemical cues that signal the presence of crabs.

To test this, Ambler collected newly settled juveniles from both bays and raised them in four sets of tanks. One set received seawater from tanks in which crabs were fed periwinkles; a second, water from tanks in which crabs were fed fish; a third, water containing crushed periwinkles but no crabs; and a fourth, plain seawater. After four months, snails in the first set had grown the thickest shells, those in the second and third sets shells of intermediate thickness, and those in the fourth the thinnest. Crucially, juveniles from Tolley Inlet and from Hesk Sound responded in the same way, so the difference between the wild populations could not reflect inherited differences between them.

The experiment also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere. Those in the first set, though better armored, had added less body tissue than the snails raised in plain seawater. Shell material laid down on the inside of the shell takes up room the snail’s body would otherwise occupy, and building it diverts energy from growth. Where crabs are absent, a thin shell is the better bargain.

Ambler’s account has not settled every question. The concentrations of crab cues in her tanks were probably higher than those snails encounter in open water, and she has not ruled out that differences in the calcium content of the two bays’ water contribute to the pattern in the wild. Still, her experiment explains what the wave hypothesis could not: why sheltered and exposed snails in Hesk Sound are alike, and why genetically indistinguishable snails in the two bays are not.

passages.title: Mirela Strand and the drifting phrase
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When the dance company founded by the choreographer Mirela Strand began reviving her works in the 1990s, its rehearsal directors confronted a puzzle. Strand, who made more than forty dances between 1948 and 1971, kept detailed notebooks, but the counts recorded in them frequently fail to fit the music. In Harbor Song (1956), for example, a recurring phrase for the full ensemble is notated in sevens, though the score that accompanies it is written throughout in a steady four. Earlier revivals treated such passages as slips of the pen and quietly regularized them, stretching or compressing the movement so that each phrase began on a downbeat.

The dance historian Tobias Arne has argued that the mismatches are no slips. Strand, he contends, built her phrases not on musical meter but on the length of a dancer’s breath, and she let movement and music run side by side as two independent cycles. Because a phrase of seven counts repeated against music in four cannot begin on a downbeat again until both cycles end at the same moment, the dancers and the score drift apart and then periodically converge. On Arne’s account, these moments of convergence were the structural joints of Strand’s dances.

Arne’s most persuasive evidence comes from the notebooks themselves. In Harbor Song the ensemble phrase is performed four times in succession; four phrases of seven counts occupy twenty-eight counts, or exactly seven measures of four, so the fifth phrase is the first since the opening to begin on a downbeat. It is precisely at that point that Strand’s notes call for the soloist’s entrance. Arne found the same pattern in eleven other dances: entrances, exits, and changes of lighting fall where movement and music realign, rather than at the beginnings of sections of the score. A rehearsal pianist who worked with Strand in the 1960s recalled that she forbade dancers to “listen for the one,” telling them instead to count their own phrases and trust that “the music will find you.” Regularizing the counts, Arne concludes, erased the very feature that organized the dances.

Arne’s theory is a considerable advance, and the company has since restored the original counts in several revivals. Yet the evidence for his claim about breath is much thinner than the evidence for the pattern of convergence. Strand never mentioned breath in her notebooks; the idea derives from a single radio interview in which she said that a phrase should be “as long as it needs to be,” a remark that could as easily refer to dramatic need as to physiological need. Moreover, in at least three of her late works the phrases never realign with the music at all, which suggests that by the end of her career Strand valued the tension of drift for its own sake rather than as a path toward convergence. Arne’s account explains how many of Strand’s dances are built; why she built them that way remains an open question.

passages.title: Kenning and the Halvey stamp scrip
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In the winter of 1932, with its two textile mills shut and its only bank closed, the town council of Halvey began paying its employees partly in scrip: paper certificates, redeemable for town taxes, that local merchants agreed to accept for goods. Halvey’s scrip carried an unusual feature. On the back of each certificate were fifty-two squares, and a certificate remained valid only if its holder affixed a one-cent stamp, purchased from the town, to the next empty square each week. In The Fast Dollar (2009), the economic historian Rhoda Kenning argues that this weekly charge, by making it costly to hold scrip, induced residents to spend it quickly, and that the resulting acceleration of exchange explains the revival of Halvey’s retail trade during the eighteen months the scrip circulated.

Kenning’s account has the merit of attending to the design of a currency rather than merely to its quantity, and her reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation from surviving stamp records is ingenious. But she does not clarify what she takes the revival to consist in. At times she points to the number of transactions recorded by Halvey’s merchants, at others to the total value of their sales. Yet the number of transactions could rise sharply even while total sales stagnated, if residents merely broke their purchases into smaller ones in order to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due.

Her argument also assumes that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did. Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise: most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes. If the scrip traveled mainly from council employees to shopkeepers and back to the treasury, it may have functioned less as a circulating currency than as a means by which the town paid its employees out of future tax receipts—a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.

Finally, Kenning does not adequately account for the experience of Corley, a town twenty miles downriver that issued scrip in 1933 without any stamp requirement. According to the records of Corley’s merchants’ association, retail sales there recovered at roughly the same rate as Halvey’s. Kenning dismisses the comparison on the ground that Corley’s economy depended on a railway repair shop that reopened that year. But the reopening of an employer is precisely the kind of factor that could also have contributed to Halvey’s recovery, since one of Halvey’s mills resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933.

None of this shows that the stamps were without effect. It suggests, rather, that their effect cannot be read directly from Halvey’s sales figures, and that the town’s experience is better evidence of what a cash-starved municipality can accomplish with its power to tax than of the virtues of money designed to lose value.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes the origins of a type of law; passage B evaluates the evidence for that law’s effectiveness.
Passage A defends a type of law against several criticisms; passage B argues that the law should be broadened.
Passage A raises several objections to a type of law; passage B defends that type of law in ways that respond to some of those objections.
Passage A argues that a type of law has failed to achieve its goals; passage B argues that those goals were mistaken.
Passage A and passage B offer competing accounts of why people are reluctant to apologize.
questions.explanation: Passage A lists three problems with apology statutes (‘First… Second… Third…’), and passage B defends such laws, answering A’s worries about unsatisfying sympathy and about other reasons people withhold apologies. That is C. D is the tempting trap: A does doubt the laws work, but B never calls the laws’ goals mistaken; it says the laws serve those goals. A, B, and E misdescribe one or both passages.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Label each passage, then find the choice that matches both labels.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of each passage, plus A’s ‘First… Second… Third…’ list.

breakdown.analysis: What is each passage doing? A: “the statutes rest on uncertain ground,” then three numbered problems. That’s a critique. B: “Critics… sometimes treat…”, then “It is true that… But…”, “Nor need such laws…”, “Finally…”. That’s a defense, and several of its points line up with A’s problems without naming A. We need: A objects, B defends.

choices.note: A doesn’t tell the history of the statutes; it attacks them. And B isn’t a neutral evaluation of evidence. It argues for the laws.
Backwards on A. A is the critic, not the defender. And B never asks for broader laws.

CORRECT. A gives three objections; B defends apology laws and answers at least two of A’s worries (unsatisfying sympathy, many reasons for not apologizing). It never answers A’s third point, which is why “some of those objections” is exactly right.

Tempting on the first half: A does think the statutes may not deliver. But B doesn’t say the goals were wrong. B says the laws help achieve them (more apologies, more settlements, more accurate verdicts).
Only one paragraph of A (the second) is about why people don’t apologize, and B doesn’t offer a competing account of that. Too narrow a description of both passages.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: an expression of sympathy that does not admit fault is of real value to many injured people
fear of litigation is one of the reasons people withhold apologies
some injured people want an admission of fault rather than only an expression of sympathy
most apology statutes protect expressions of sympathy but not admissions of fault
jurors tend to interpret expressions of sympathy as admissions of fault
questions.explanation: Passage A says a sympathy-only apology is the kind injured people find ‘least satisfying’ and ‘gives injured people little of what they actually seek,’ while passage B says that for many injured people ‘what matters first is acknowledgment’ and backs it with Castan’s settlement finding. That is a direct disagreement, A. B and C are points both authors accept, D is stated by A and is consistent with B, and E is the trap: B asserts it, but A says nothing about how jurors hear apologies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: A’s second paragraph (sympathy-only apologies give injured people little of what they seek) against B’s second paragraph (acknowledgment matters first; Castan’s study).

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Silence on one side doesn’t count. So for each choice, check both passages. The clash is the value of sympathy-only apologies to the injured. A: they’re the “least satisfying” kind and give injured people “little of what they actually seek.” B: for many, “what matters first is acknowledgment,” and claimants who got sympathy with no admission were more willing to settle. Note A’s third objection doesn’t change this: A thinks weightless regret can be used to make claims go away, not that it gives the injured anything of real value.

choices.note: CORRECT. A says a sympathy-only apology gives injured people little of what they seek; B says acknowledgment is what many of them want first. Yes versus no on the same question.
Both agree. A says physicians cited other reasons “at least as often as legal exposure,” so legal exposure is one reason. B says removing “one of those reasons still helps.”
Both agree. A says the statutes promote the apology people “find least satisfying,” and B concedes “some injured people want the latter.”
A states this outright, and B accepts it (“a protected statement of sympathy is not a confession of fault”). No disagreement.
Tempting, since this is B’s argument and A is the critic. But A never discusses jurors or how they hear apologies. You can’t disagree with a point you never address.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the physicians whom Halvik asked about medical errors
choices: apologized less often than other hospital staff did
said they would apologize more readily if apology statutes were adopted
cited legal exposure more often than any other reason for not apologizing
gave reasons other than legal exposure for not apologizing
reported that institutional habit discouraged patients from suing
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says the physicians cited embarrassment, uncertainty, and institutional habit ‘at least as often as legal exposure,’ so they gave reasons other than legal exposure, D. C is the trap: ‘at least as often’ means legal exposure was not cited more often than the others. A, B, and E mention things the passage never states.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about Halvik’s interviews.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Go back and read the sentence. Physicians “cited embarrassment, uncertainty about what had gone wrong, and institutional habit at least as often as legal exposure.” So legal exposure was one reason, and there were others that came up just as much. We want the choice that says that, nothing more.

choices.note: Halvik asked physicians only. No comparison to other staff appears anywhere.
Nothing about what they’d do under a statute. If anything, A uses Halvik to suggest the statutes won’t change much.
Reverses the finding. “At least as often as legal exposure” means legal exposure did not come out on top.
CORRECT. Embarrassment, uncertainty, and habit are all reasons other than legal exposure, and the passage says the physicians cited them.
Institutional habit was a reason physicians didn’t apologize. It has nothing to do with patients deciding not to sue. Right words, wrong relationship.

questions.stem: In saying that ‘sincerity is not measured by legal risk’ (first paragraph of passage B), the author of passage B most probably means that
choices: apologies that carry no legal risk are usually more sincere than those that do
whether an apology is heartfelt does not depend on whether it could be used against the person who offers it
courts are not in a position to determine whether an apology is sincere
people who apologize at the scene of an accident rarely consider the legal consequences of doing so
an apology that carries legal risk is less likely to be offered than one that does not
questions.explanation: The phrase answers critics who suppose an apology can be sincere ‘only when it is costly’; B’s author replies that a protected apology can be fully meant, as with the driver who ‘may mean it entirely, whether or not the words could later be read to a jury.’ That is B. A overcorrects by making protected apologies more sincere, and E states the statutes’ rationale, which is true in spirit but not what this phrase means.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Translate the phrase in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph: the critics’ view right before the phrase and the driver example right after it.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before: critics act “as if an expression of regret could be sincere only when it is costly.” The phrase is the reply. Then the driver example: he “may mean it entirely,” jury or no jury. So: legal risk and sincerity are unrelated. Risk doesn’t make an apology sincere, and the lack of risk doesn’t make it fake. We want “sincerity doesn’t depend on legal risk.”

choices.note: Too strong. B says sincerity doesn’t depend on risk, not that low-risk apologies are more sincere. That just flips the critics’ error.
CORRECT. Heartfelt or not is a separate question from whether the words could be used in court. That’s exactly what the driver example shows.
Courts and their abilities never come up here. The point is about apologies, not judges.
B says the driver may be sincere “whether or not” the words could be used. It doesn’t claim people don’t think about consequences.
Tempting, because this is the idea behind apology laws. But this phrase is about sincerity, not about how often people apologize.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions a seatbelt law (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that apology statutes, like seatbelt laws, will eventually be adopted in nearly every jurisdiction
show that laws intended to change people’s behavior are seldom fully effective
provide evidence that fear of legal consequences is the main reason people fail to apologize
illustrate the difficulty of measuring the effects of a law
illustrate the claim that a measure can be worthwhile even if it addresses only one cause of a problem
questions.explanation: The seatbelt example backs the sentence before it: if people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one still helps. Seatbelts don’t prevent every death, yet no one calls the law pointless, which is E. B is the trap; the example concedes that laws are not complete solutions, but its point is that partial help is still worth having, not that such laws generally fail. C contradicts B’s concession that there are many reasons.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the seatbelt example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, third paragraph, read against passage A’s third paragraph (many reasons physicians don’t apologize).

breakdown.analysis: Why mention seatbelts in a passage about apologies? It’s an analogy. The claim right before it: “If people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one of those reasons still helps.” Seatbelts don’t stop every death, but the law isn’t pointless. Same for apology laws: they remove only one obstacle (fear of being sued), but that’s still worth something. This answers A’s second point, that “a rule of evidence can do nothing” about the other reasons.

choices.note: Nothing about adoption trends. The example is about whether partial help is worthwhile.
Tempting, because the example admits seatbelts don’t prevent every death. But the point is the opposite of “laws seldom work”: it’s that a partly effective law is still worthwhile.
B grants that there are “many reasons.” The example doesn’t make legal fear the main one.
Measurement isn’t the issue. The example assumes we know seatbelts help.
CORRECT. One cause removed, problem not fully solved, measure still worth having. That’s the seatbelt point, applied to apology laws.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be most likely to offer regarding the study by Castan described in passage B?
choices: Claimants in mediated disputes are unlike most injured people, since most injured people never enter mediation.
Expressions of sympathy that carry no admission of fault are rarely sincere.
Claimants may have been more willing to settle only because they feared that the expressions of sympathy would be used against them.
That claimants were more willing to accept settlement offers does not show that the claims they gave up were ones they should have given up.
The study shows only that apology statutes increase the number of apologies offered, not that they reduce lawsuits.
questions.explanation: B presents Castan’s finding (sympathy made claimants more willing to settle) as a point in favor of apology laws. A’s third objection is that weightless expressions of regret may ‘defuse claims that deserve to be pursued,’ so A’s author would say that easier settlement is not a good result in itself, which is D. A is the strongest trap, a generic sampling complaint that nothing in passage A supports. B is the view passage B attributes to critics, but A’s author never questions anyone’s sincerity; C is incoherent, and E misdescribes the study.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the objection A’s author would raise to B’s use of the Castan study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph (Castan) against passage A’s last paragraph (strategic use).

breakdown.analysis: B treats “more willing to accept settlement offers” as good news. Ask: good for whom? A’s third problem says an insurer can use weightless regret to “defuse claims that deserve to be pursued.” From A’s side, Castan’s result could be exactly that problem in action. People settled, but maybe they shouldn’t have. It’s like a store showing that customers stop complaining after a friendly apology. That proves the apology works on customers, not that their complaints were wrong. The answer must come from A’s own concerns, not just any criticism you could think of.

choices.note: The big trap. It sounds like a sharp methodological point. But A never mentions mediation or who ends up in it. This criticism comes from you, not from A’s author.

Tempting, because B says critics treat these apologies as insincere. But that’s B’s characterization. A’s author never questions sincerity; A’s first problem is that such apologies are unsatisfying, not fake.
Makes no sense. The sympathy in the study carried no admission, and fear of its use would push people away from settling, not toward it.
CORRECT. This is A’s third objection aimed at B’s evidence: settlement may just mean a deserving claim was defused, which is what A fears these laws make possible.
Misdescribes the study. Castan measured willingness to settle, not how many apologies were offered under a statute.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the use of apology statutes that passage A describes as ‘most troubling’ (last paragraph of passage A)?
choices: A retailer trains its staff to offer scripted expressions of concern, which a consumer law makes inadmissible in court, so that customers with valid complaints will be less likely to demand refunds.
A hospital encourages its physicians to admit their errors openly, even though doing so increases the hospital’s exposure to lawsuits.
A city protects bystanders from liability when they give aid at accident scenes, and more bystanders begin to offer aid.
A landlord refuses to apologize to tenants for a flood because he fears that an apology would be used against him in court.
A driver apologizes after a collision and later learns that a statute prevents the apology from being used as evidence.
questions.explanation: The ‘most troubling’ use is an insurer coaching policyholders to give legally weightless regret in order to defuse claims that deserve to be pursued: a protection meant for genuine apology is exploited to make valid claims go away. A matches every element. D is the trap, since it is also about apologies and lawsuits, but it describes the reluctance the statutes were meant to cure, not their exploitation; C and E show the law working as intended, and B involves no protection at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of A’s third problem in a new setting.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Break the scenario into parts: 1. a legal protection meant to encourage genuine apology; 2. someone with an interest in limiting payouts coaches people to use it; 3. the apologies are carefully emptied of legal weight; 4. the goal is to make deserving claims disappear. We want a case with all four, especially the cynical use and the valid claims.

choices.note: CORRECT. Protected, scripted concern (1–3), used so that customers with valid complaints back off (4). That’s the insurer’s move in a store.
The opposite: real admissions despite legal risk. No protection is being gamed.
This is the protection doing what it’s supposed to do. Nothing strategic or cynical.
Tempting because it’s about apologies and lawsuits. But this is the original problem the statutes address (fear of liability), not their misuse.
A sincere apology that happens to be protected. No coaching, no aim of defeating a valid claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Periwinkles in Hesk Sound have thicker shells than those in Tolley Inlet because Hesk Sound is more exposed to storm waves.
Although they are genetically indistinguishable, the periwinkles of Hesk Sound and Tolley Inlet have evolved different shell thicknesses in response to different predators.
Ambler’s experiment shows that building a thick shell slows a periwinkle’s growth, which explains why most periwinkles have thin shells.
The thickness of a periwinkle’s shell depends mainly on the calcium content of the water in which it grows.

Experimental evidence supports Ambler’s view that the difference in shell thickness between the two bays reflects each snail’s response to chemical cues signaling crabs, though some questions remain open.
questions.explanation: The passage presents Ambler’s hypothesis that snails thicken their shells in response to crab cues, describes the experiment supporting it, and ends by noting open questions while affirming that it explains what the wave hypothesis could not. That is E. B is the trap: ‘evolved’ implies inherited differences, which the experiment rules out. A is the view Ambler rejects, C is a detail from the fourth paragraph, and D is only a possibility the author raises.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the sentence that sums up the whole passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (Ambler’s proposal) and the last paragraph (the verdict).

breakdown.analysis: Puzzle: same genes, different shells. Old answer: waves. Ambler: no, it’s crab cues, and each snail adjusts its own shell. Experiment backs her. Last paragraph: some questions left, “still” her account explains what the wave idea couldn’t. The main point should have Ambler’s idea, the support for it, and a slight hedge.

choices.note: That’s the old view, the one Ambler rejects with the sheltered-cove evidence.
Tempting, but “evolved” is the problem. Evolution means inherited differences. The experiment shows juveniles from both bays responded the same way, so the difference is not inherited.
One detail from the fourth paragraph, and it overstates: the passage never says most periwinkles have thin shells.
The author mentions calcium only as something Ambler hasn’t ruled out. Not the main point, and not supported as the main cause.
CORRECT. Ambler’s cue hypothesis, supported by the experiment, with the author’s noted reservations. That covers the whole passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following led Ambler to doubt that exposure to storm waves explains the thickness of Hesk Sound periwinkles’ shells?
choices: Genetic surveys revealed no differences between the periwinkles of the two bays.
Periwinkles in sheltered parts of Hesk Sound have shells as thick as those of periwinkles in exposed parts.
Tolley Inlet is as exposed to storm waves as Hesk Sound is.
Thick-shelled periwinkles add less body tissue than thin-shelled periwinkles do.
A shell-crushing crab has never become established in Tolley Inlet.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Ambler doubted the wave account and immediately gives her reason: within Hesk Sound, snails in sheltered coves have shells as thick as those on exposed headlands, which is B. E is the trap; the crab’s absence from Tolley Inlet is part of her alternative explanation, not her reason for rejecting the wave account. A is background, C contradicts the first paragraph, and D comes from the later experiment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the specific observation that made Ambler doubt the wave explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: “Ambler doubted this account. Within Hesk Sound itself, she noted…” The very next sentence is the reason. If waves made shells thick, sheltered snails should have thinner shells than exposed ones. They don’t. That’s the evidence against waves.

choices.note: Background from the first paragraph. Genetic sameness doesn’t, by itself, count against waves, and the passage doesn’t present it as Ambler’s reason.
CORRECT. Same thickness in sheltered and exposed spots means wave exposure isn’t what’s driving thickness.
Contradicts the passage: Hesk Sound is “more exposed to storm waves.”
This is a later experimental result about the cost of thick shells. It didn’t lead her to doubt the wave idea.
Tempting, since it’s part of her reasoning. But it supports her crab hypothesis; the stem asks what made her doubt the wave hypothesis.

questions.stem: In saying that where crabs are absent ‘a thin shell is the better bargain’ (end of the fourth paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: thin shells cost periwinkles less to produce than they cost other snails
periwinkles in places without crabs are protected by their faster growth
without the threat of crabs, the protection a thick shell offers is not worth what it costs the snail in growth
where crabs are absent, thin-shelled periwinkles are less likely than thick-shelled ones to be dislodged by waves
periwinkles that move to places without crabs lose the extra layers of their shells
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph describes a trade-off: a thick shell protects against crabs but takes up body space and diverts energy from growth. Where crabs are absent, the protection buys nothing, so the cost isn’t worth paying, which is C. B is the trap: faster growth is the benefit of a thin shell, but the passage never says growth protects the snail. A, D, and E bring in comparisons or processes the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Translate ‘better bargain’ using the costs and benefits in the paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A bargain is a cost-benefit judgment. Cost of a thick shell: less room for body, energy taken from growth. Benefit: armor against crabs. No crabs, no benefit, so you’d be paying for nothing. A thin shell lets the snail keep its growth. We want “without crabs, a thick shell isn’t worth its cost.”

choices.note: No comparison to other snails anywhere. “Bargain” here compares thick and thin shells for the same snail.
Tempting: faster growth is what thin shells buy. But the passage doesn’t say growth protects the snail from anything. The bargain is growth versus armor you don’t need.
CORRECT. Armor’s only payoff is against crabs; without them, the growth cost isn’t worth it.
Waves are the rejected hypothesis, and the paragraph says nothing about dislodging.
The passage never says snails can shed shell layers. It talks about how shells are built as snails grow.

questions.stem: The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
choices: draw on an additional result of the experiment described in the third paragraph to explain why the response it documents does not occur everywhere
present evidence that undermines the explanation favored by earlier researchers
identify a limitation of the experiment described in the third paragraph
describe the chemical process by which crab cues cause periwinkles to thicken their shells
introduce a rival hypothesis that the author goes on to reject
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by saying the experiment ‘also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere,’ then uses the finding that thick-shelled snails added less body tissue to explain the cost of thickening. That is A. B describes the second paragraph and C the fifth; D is the trap, because the paragraph explains how shell building costs the snail, not how crab cues trigger it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the fourth paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first sentence, and how it connects to the third.

breakdown.analysis: Use the paragraph’s first sentence as the label: the experiment “also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere.” So: same experiment, new result (less body tissue), used to answer a natural question (if thick shells protect, why not always build them?). The answer is cost.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same experiment, an extra finding (less body tissue), used to explain why snails don’t thicken their shells everywhere.
That’s the second paragraph’s job (sheltered coves vs. exposed headlands). The fourth paragraph doesn’t mention waves.
That’s the fifth paragraph (cue concentrations, calcium). The fourth paragraph reports a result, not a limitation.
Tempting, since the paragraph does describe shell material being laid down. But it explains what thickening costs, not how the crab cue triggers it. No chemistry of the cue appears.
No rival hypothesis appears here. The wave hypothesis was dealt with earlier.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The cues from crabs fed periwinkles produced the thickest shells because they were the most concentrated cues used in the experiment.
Adult periwinkles moved from Hesk Sound to Tolley Inlet would soon develop shells as thin as those of Tolley Inlet periwinkles.
Periwinkles raised in water containing crushed periwinkles grew thinner shells than those raised in water from tanks of crabs fed fish.
Cues from crabs alone are sufficient to produce shells as thick as those of wild periwinkles in Hesk Sound.
A periwinkle can respond to signs of injured members of its own species even in the absence of any cue from crabs.
questions.explanation: In the third tank set, water held crushed periwinkles but no crabs, and those snails grew shells of intermediate thickness, thicker than the plain-seawater controls. So periwinkles respond to cues from injured periwinkles even without crab cues, which is E. C is the trap: the passage puts the second and third sets together at ‘intermediate thickness’ and gives no ranking between them. A invents a cause, B assumes shells can thin, and D compares tank snails to wild ones, which the passage never does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the experiment’s results actually support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph: the four tank sets and their results.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so lay out the results. 1. Crabs fed periwinkles → thickest. 2. Crabs fed fish → intermediate. 3. Crushed periwinkles, no crabs → intermediate. 4. Plain seawater → thinnest. Set 3 has no crab cue at all, yet beats plain seawater. So the snails react to crushed periwinkles on their own. Watch for answers that rank sets 2 and 3 or explain why set 1 won; the passage gives neither.

choices.note: Invents a cause. The passage never says set 1 had more concentrated cues. The simpler reading is that it combined crab cues with cues from eaten periwinkles.
We don’t know this. The passage never says shells can thin, and adults in particular have already laid down their shell material.
Tempting, since you might expect crab cues to matter more. But the passage lumps sets 2 and 3 together as “intermediate thickness.” No ranking between them is given.
No comparison between tank shells and wild Hesk Sound shells is made, so “sufficient to match the wild” is unsupported.
CORRECT. Set 3 had crushed periwinkles but no crabs, and its snails still grew thicker shells than the plain-seawater set.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Ambler’s explanation of the difference in shell thickness between the periwinkles of the two bays?
choices: In a third bay on the Varn Peninsula where the crab is common, periwinkles also have thick shells.
Throughout Hesk Sound, the concentration of crab cues in the water is far below the level needed to produce any measurable change in periwinkle shells.
Periwinkles on Hesk Sound’s exposed headlands are more often dislodged by waves than are those in its sheltered coves.
In Ambler’s tanks, thick-shelled periwinkles were more likely than thin-shelled periwinkles to survive attacks by crabs.
The water of Tolley Inlet contains less dissolved calcium than that of Hesk Sound, and periwinkles raised in low-calcium water build somewhat thinner shells.
questions.explanation: Ambler’s explanation needs wild Hesk Sound snails to be exposed to enough crab cue to trigger thickening; the last paragraph already worries that tank concentrations exceeded those in open water. If cue levels everywhere in the sound are too low to have any effect, her mechanism cannot be what thickens the wild shells, so B seriously undermines it. E is the trap: it adds a possible contributing factor, which the author already allows, without showing that crab cues do not also work. A and D support Ambler, and C is irrelevant to the cue account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the crab-cue explanation of the wild difference.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fifth paragraph (cue concentrations, calcium) and the second paragraph (her hypothesis).

breakdown.analysis: Ambler’s experiment shows snails can respond to crab cues in tanks. Her explanation says that’s why wild Hesk Sound snails are thick. Gap: are wild snails actually exposed to enough cue? The author flags this: tank levels were “probably higher” than in open water. So attack that link. If the sound’s cue levels are too low to do anything, the tank result can’t explain the wild pattern. It’s like proving a drug works at ten times the dose people actually take.

choices.note: Strengthens. Another crab bay with thick shells fits Ambler’s pattern.
CORRECT. If wild cue levels are below the threshold for any effect, crab cues can’t be what makes Hesk Sound shells thick, whatever happens in tanks.
Irrelevant. Dislodging rates don’t bear on what controls shell thickness, and Ambler already showed sheltered and exposed shells are alike.
Strengthens the logic of her account: thick shells really are useful against crabs.

Tempting, since calcium is the alternative the author mentions. But it shows only that calcium may contribute a little (“somewhat thinner”). Both factors could operate, so Ambler’s crab account survives. B, by contrast, removes her mechanism entirely.

questions.stem: Which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether the difference in calcium content mentioned in the last paragraph contributes to the difference in shell thickness between the two bays’ periwinkles?
choices: raising juveniles from both bays in plain seawater and comparing the thickness of their shells
raising juveniles in water from tanks of crabs fed periwinkles at several different concentrations and comparing the thickness of their shells
comparing the shell thickness of periwinkles in sheltered and exposed parts of Tolley Inlet
raising juveniles, with no crab cues present, in seawater matched to the calcium content of Hesk Sound and in seawater matched to that of Tolley Inlet, and comparing the thickness of their shells
measuring the calcium content of shells collected from each of the two bays
questions.explanation: To learn whether calcium matters, vary calcium while holding everything else, including crab cues, constant; D does exactly that with the two bays’ calcium levels. B is the trap, because it tests the other reservation in the last paragraph, cue concentration, not calcium. A repeats the test for inherited differences, C tests waves, and E measures shell composition without showing what causes thickness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the experiment that isolates calcium as a cause of thickness.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fifth paragraph (the calcium reservation), using the third paragraph’s experiment as a model.

breakdown.analysis: To test one factor, change only that factor. Here: two calcium levels (Hesk’s and Tolley’s), same snails, no crab cues to muddy things, then compare shells. If the Hesk-level calcium gives thicker shells, calcium contributes. If not, it doesn’t. Anything that varies something else, or just measures shells, can’t answer the question.

choices.note: Tests whether the populations differ genetically, which the original experiment already covered. Calcium isn’t varied.
Tempting, because cue concentration is the other worry in the same sentence. But this varies the crab cue, not calcium.
Waves, not calcium. And it compares spots within one bay.
CORRECT. Calcium is the only thing that changes, and crab cues are kept out. Any shell difference would show calcium’s effect.
Shell calcium tells you what shells are made of, not whether the water’s calcium makes shells thicker.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Arne has shown that Strand built her phrases on the length of a dancer’s breath, and the company was therefore right to restore the original counts in its revivals.
The counts in Strand’s notebooks that fail to fit the music were long mistaken for errors, but they in fact reflect Strand’s indifference to the scores her dances were set to.
Arne convincingly explains the mismatched counts in Strand’s notebooks as a deliberate structural device, though his claim about the source of that device is less well supported.
Strand’s late works, in which the phrases never realign with the music, show that Arne’s account of how she organized her dances is mistaken.
Earlier revivals regularized Strand’s counts because their directors lacked the testimony of musicians who had worked with her, testimony that Arne has now supplied.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the puzzle of the mismatched counts (first paragraph), Arne’s convergence theory and its evidence (second and third), and then a reservation: the breath claim is thinly supported and the motive remains open (fourth). C captures both the endorsement and the reservation. A is the tempting trap, but it treats the breath claim as proven, which is exactly what the author doubts. D overstates the late works, which only suggest a change in Strand’s aims late in her career.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one sentence the whole passage is built to support, including the author’s reservation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of P2 (Arne’s claim) and the whole of P4 (‘considerable advance’ … ‘Yet’ … ‘remains an open question’).

breakdown.analysis: So is the author on Arne’s side or not? Both. P3 calls his evidence ‘persuasive,’ P4 calls the theory ‘a considerable advance,’ and then the ‘Yet’ arrives: the breath part is thin, and why Strand built dances this way is still open. That’s the classic measured LSAT attitude: favorable with a reservation. We need an answer that says: Arne is right that the mismatches are deliberate structure, but his explanation of where they come from is weaker.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds pro-Arne, and the company did restore the counts. But it says Arne ‘has shown’ the breath claim, and P4 says that’s exactly the weak part. An answer that endorses the part the author doubts is wrong.
Wrong. Nobody says Strand was indifferent to the music. Arne says movement and music were designed to drift and then converge, which means she cared a lot about where they meet.
CORRECT. Endorsement (the mismatches are a deliberate device that organizes the dances) plus reservation (the breath explanation is less well supported). That’s P2–P3 and P4 in one sentence.

Too strong. The late works suggest Strand’s aims changed late in her career; they don’t sink Arne’s account of the many dances where the convergence pattern holds. The author still says Arne ‘explains how many of Strand’s dances are built.’

We don’t know this. The passage never says why earlier directors regularized the counts beyond treating them as ‘slips of the pen,’ and the pianist’s memory is one piece of Arne’s evidence, not the point of the passage.

questions.stem: In the passage, the phrase “listen for the one” (third paragraph) most probably refers to
choices: attending to the first beat of each musical measure as a cue for starting a phrase
matching each movement in a phrase to a separate note of the melody
taking the timing of the ensemble from a single lead dancer
anticipating the beginning of each new section of the score
counting each phrase from its first movement rather than from its last
questions.explanation: Strand told dancers not to ‘listen for the one’ but to count their own phrases and let ‘the music … find you’; the thing she rejected is the practice the earlier revivals imposed, beginning every phrase on a downbeat (first paragraph), which is A. D is tempting because the third paragraph mentions ‘the beginnings of sections of the score,’ but that phrase concerns where Arne found entrances do not fall, not what dancers were told to listen for. E misreads ‘count their own phrases’ as a rule about where to start counting.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what Strand was telling dancers not to do when she forbade them to ‘listen for the one.’

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The pianist’s recollection near the end of P3, read against the last sentence of P1 (phrases regularized to begin ‘on a downbeat’).

breakdown.analysis: Read the instruction as a contrast: don’t listen for the one; instead, count your own phrases and trust the music to find you. So ‘the one’ must be something in the music that dancers would normally use to time their phrases. P1 tells us what that is: the earlier revivals made ‘each phrase began on a downbeat.’ The downbeat is the first beat of a measure, count ‘one.’ We need an answer that says: waiting for the music’s first beat to start a phrase.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘The one’ is the downbeat, the first beat of a measure. Strand didn’t want dancers lining phrases up with it; she wanted them on their own count so the drift could happen. That’s exactly what the earlier revivals undid.
Wrong. Nothing in the passage is about melody notes. The issue is meter (counts and measures), not matching steps to tunes.
Wrong. The alternative Strand gave was ‘count their own phrases,’ which points away from following anyone else, dancer or musician. No lead dancer is mentioned.

Tempting. P3 does mention ‘the beginnings of sections of the score.’ But that’s Arne’s finding about where entrances don’t fall, not Strand’s instruction to dancers. And ‘the one’ in a passage about counts and measures is a beat, not a section.
Wrong. This twists ‘count their own phrases’ into a rule about which end to count from. The contrast is between the dancer’s own count and the music’s count, not between ends of a phrase.

questions.stem: According to the passage, earlier revivals of Strand’s dances
choices: restored the counts recorded in Strand’s notebooks wherever they conflicted with the music
relied on films of the original performances rather than on Strand’s notebooks
set Strand’s choreography to newly arranged scores written in four
moved the soloist’s entrance in Harbor Song to the beginning of a section of the score
altered the movement so that each phrase would begin on a downbeat
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says earlier revivals treated the mismatches as slips and regularized them, ‘stretching or compressing the movement so that each phrase began on a downbeat,’ which is E. A reverses the history: restoring the original counts is what the company did later, after Arne (fourth paragraph). B, C and D describe things the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the earlier revivals did.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of P1.

breakdown.analysis: This one is a straight lookup. P1: earlier revivals ‘treated such passages as slips of the pen and quietly regularized them, stretching or compressing the movement so that each phrase began on a downbeat.’ We need an answer that says they changed the movement to fit the downbeat.

choices.note: Opposite. Restoring the original counts is what the company did after Arne’s work (first sentence of P4). The earlier revivals did the reverse.
Wrong. Films are never mentioned. The earlier directors worked from the notebooks; that’s how they knew the counts didn’t fit.
Wrong. The scores weren’t changed; the movement was. The music was already ‘in a steady four.’
We don’t know this. Nothing says the earlier revivals moved the soloist’s entrance. ‘Sections of the score’ comes from Arne’s finding in P3, not from a description of earlier revivals.
CORRECT. Nearly word for word from P1: they stretched or compressed the movement so each phrase began on a downbeat.

questions.stem: The author mentions the radio interview (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that Strand intended the phrases of her late works never to realign with the music
indicate that the main support for Arne’s claim about breath is open to another interpretation
show that Strand spoke more openly about her working methods late in her career than earlier
suggest that Strand regarded the dramatic content of her dances as more important than their structure
explain why rehearsal directors at first regarded the mismatched counts as errors
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the breath idea ‘derives from a single radio interview’ and that Strand’s remark ‘could as easily refer to dramatic need as to physiological need,’ so the interview is cited to show that the sole basis for the breath claim is ambiguous: B. D is the tempting trap because it picks up the word ‘dramatic,’ but the author only says the remark could refer to dramatic need, not that Strand ranked drama above structure. A attaches the interview to the late works, which are a separate point introduced by ‘Moreover.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the radio interview.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Sentences two and three of P4: ‘Yet the evidence for his claim about breath is much thinner…’ and the interview sentence after it.

breakdown.analysis: Why mention an interview at all? Look at the sentence just before it: the evidence for breath is ‘much thinner.’ Then the interview is offered as the only source for the breath idea, and the author says the quote could mean dramatic need just as easily as physical need. So the interview is the weak foundation, and the author is showing it can be read another way. Prephrase: to show that the breath claim rests on one ambiguous remark.

choices.note: Wrong paragraph job. The late works come up in the next sentence, after ‘Moreover,’ as a separate point. The interview is about breath, not about phrases that never realign.

CORRECT. The interview is the single source of the breath idea, and the author points out that the key remark fits a dramatic reading just as well. That’s showing the main support is open to another interpretation.
Wrong. We aren’t told when the interview happened, and nothing compares how openly she spoke early versus late. The point is the opposite: she said very little about method.

Tempting. It borrows ‘dramatic’ from the passage. But the author only says the remark ‘could as easily refer to dramatic need.’ Could is not did, and nothing says drama mattered more to her than structure. Too strong.
Wrong. The early directors’ view comes from P1 and has nothing to do with the interview. The interview bears on Arne’s explanation, not on the earlier revivals.

questions.stem: Suppose a newly discovered notebook of Strand’s records an ensemble phrase of five counts that is performed several times in succession against music written throughout in three, with the first performance of the phrase beginning on a downbeat. If Arne’s account is correct, the notebook would be most likely to place a soloist’s entrance at the beginning of the
choices: third performance of the phrase
fifth performance of the phrase
fifth measure of the music
fourth performance of the phrase
seventh measure of the music
questions.explanation: On Arne’s account entrances fall where movement and music realign (third paragraph). Three phrases of five counts take fifteen counts, exactly five measures of three, so the fourth performance is the first since the opening to begin on a downbeat: D. B and E copy numbers from Harbor Song (the fifth phrase, seven measures), which worked only because that phrase was in seven against four; here the fifth performance starts on count 21 and the seventh measure on count 19, neither of which is a realignment point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Arne’s rule to a new case: where do phrase and music first line up again?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of P2 (the two cycles drift and converge) and the Harbor Song arithmetic at the start of P3.

breakdown.analysis: Don’t copy the Harbor Song answer. Rebuild the rule: an entrance comes when a new phrase starts on a downbeat, which happens when the counts used so far fill a whole number of measures. Phrases of 5 against measures of 3: 1. After 1 phrase: 5 counts (not a multiple of 3). 2. After 2: 10 (no). 3. After 3: 15 = 5 measures (yes). So the fourth performance starts on count 16, the downbeat of measure 6. That’s the first convergence, and Arne says entrances go there. Check: Harbor Song is the same logic, 4 × 7 = 28 = 7 × 4, so the fifth phrase.

choices.note: Wrong. The third performance starts on count 11. Ten counts used so far isn’t a multiple of 3, so it lands mid-measure.

Tempting. It’s the Harbor Song answer: there the fifth phrase was the entrance. But that came from 7 against 4. Here the fifth performance starts on count 21, after 20 counts, and 20 isn’t a multiple of 3. You can’t transfer the number, only the rule.
Wrong. Measure 5 starts on count 13. Twelve counts used isn’t a multiple of 5, so no phrase starts there; movement and music are still apart.

CORRECT. Three phrases of five = 15 counts = five measures of three, so the fourth performance is the first since the opening to begin on a downbeat. Arne says entrances fall at exactly these realignment points.
Tempting. ‘Seven measures’ is the Harbor Song number. Here measure 7 starts on count 19; 18 counts used isn’t a multiple of 5, so it’s the middle of a phrase.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about Arne’s account?
choices: It is undermined by the rehearsal pianist’s recollection, which suggests that Strand did not expect her dancers to count their phrases.
It shows that the phrases in Strand’s late works were constructed on the same principle as those in Harbor Song.
It should not have led the company to restore the original counts until Arne’s claim about breath had been confirmed.
It fails to explain why the entrances and lighting changes in many of Strand’s dances occur where they do.
It is better supported as a description of how many of Strand’s dances are organized than as an explanation of why she organized them that way.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the evidence for the breath claim is ‘much thinner’ than the evidence for the convergence pattern and ends: Arne ‘explains how many of Strand’s dances are built; why she built them that way remains an open question,’ which is E. C is the most tempting trap because the author does doubt the breath claim, but the restoration rests on the convergence pattern, which the author accepts; nothing suggests the author faults the company. B contradicts the point about the late works, and D contradicts the third paragraph’s evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement about Arne’s theory that matches the author’s precise mix of praise and doubt.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All of P4, especially its second sentence and its last sentence; P3 for what the author calls ‘persuasive.’

breakdown.analysis: The author splits Arne’s theory in two. Part one, the convergence pattern (how the dances are built): strong, ‘persuasive,’ a ‘considerable advance.’ Part two, the breath claim (why she did it): thin, and ‘why she built them that way remains an open question.’ We need an answer that keeps that split: the how is well supported, the why is not.

choices.note: Opposite. The pianist’s recollection is part of Arne’s support: Strand told dancers to ‘count their own phrases.’ It fits the theory; it doesn’t undermine it.

Contradicts P4. In the late works the phrases ‘never realign with the music at all,’ which the author takes as a change in Strand’s aims. That’s not the Harbor Song principle of drifting toward convergence.

Tempting. The author does doubt the breath claim. But restoring the counts depends on the convergence pattern, which is the well-supported part; you don’t need to know why Strand drifted to know the counts weren’t slips. The author mentions the restoration approvingly, right next to ‘considerable advance.’
Opposite. Explaining where entrances, exits, and lighting changes fall is exactly what the theory does well (P3: they fall ‘where movement and music realign’).
CORRECT. This is the last sentence of P4 restated: Arne explains how many dances are built; why she built them that way is still open. The ‘many’ even matches the author’s hedge about the late works.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Halvey’s scrip failed to revive the town’s retail trade, because merchants returned most certificates to the treasury instead of spending them.
Kenning’s claim that Halvey’s stamp requirement explains the town’s retail revival rests on an unclear notion of revival, a doubtful assumption, and an inadequate treatment of a comparable case.
Kenning’s study of Halvey shows that the design of a currency matters more to economic recovery than does the quantity of money in circulation.
The reopening of local employers, rather than the issuing of scrip, explains the recovery of retail sales in both Halvey and Corley.
Kenning’s reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation is ingenious, but the stamp records on which it depends cannot distinguish residents’ purchases from merchants’ tax payments.
questions.explanation: After presenting Kenning’s thesis, the author faults it in three steps: she does not clarify what the revival consists in (second paragraph), she assumes merchants passed scrip on (third), and she dismisses the Corley comparison too quickly (fourth); the last paragraph says only that the stamps’ effect cannot be read from the sales figures. That is B. D is the most tempting trap, but the author says only that a reopened employer ‘could also have contributed,’ and the last paragraph refuses to conclude that the stamps had no effect. A also overstates: the author never says the trade failed to revive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point: the claim the whole passage supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of P1 (Kenning’s thesis), the opening of P2 (‘does not clarify’), P3 (‘also assumes’), P4 (‘Finally’), and the hedge in P5 (‘None of this shows…’).

breakdown.analysis: This is the ‘scholar’s view, then what it fails to clarify, what it assumes, and what it can’t handle’ structure. The target is Kenning’s explanation of the revival, not the scrip itself and not the town. And P5 is careful: the stamps may have had some effect; you just can’t prove it from the sales figures. Prephrase: Kenning’s stamp explanation has three problems, so the sales figures don’t establish it.

choices.note: Too strong. The author never says trade didn’t revive; Corley’s and Halvey’s sales both ‘recovered.’ And the merchants’ tax payments are used to question Kenning’s mechanism, not to say the scrip failed.
CORRECT. Right target (Kenning’s claim about the stamps), and it lists all three criticisms: unclear ‘revival’ (P2), the merchants assumption (P3), and the brushed-off Corley comparison (P4).
Wrong. The author credits Kenning for attending to design, but the whole passage argues her case isn’t proven. This turns a compliment into the thesis.

Tempting. P4 does raise reopened employers. But the author says that ‘could also have contributed,’ and P5 says ‘None of this shows that the stamps were without effect.’ This claims a cause the author never commits to.
Wrong. The author calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious’ and never attacks the stamp records. The merchants’ tax payments come from ‘Kenning’s own figures,’ so the records are being used, not doubted.

questions.stem: According to the passage, most of Halvey’s scrip certificates
choices: were held by residents for several months before being spent
were tendered by council employees directly in payment of their property taxes
lost their validity because their holders failed to affix the required stamps
were returned to the town treasury by merchants in payment of property taxes
passed through the hands of several merchants before reaching the treasury
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that ‘most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes,’ which is D. B is the tempting wrong-party trap: the employees received the scrip, but it was the merchants who paid it back in taxes. E contradicts the point of that paragraph, which is that merchants did not pass scrip on.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says happened to most certificates.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second sentence of P3.

breakdown.analysis: Lookup question, but watch who does what. The path in P3 is: council employees → shopkeepers → treasury, and it’s the merchants who hand the certificates in, as property-tax payments, ‘within a few weeks.’ We need an answer with the merchants and the taxes.

choices.note: Opposite. The stamp charge pushed people to spend fast, and most certificates were back at the treasury ‘within a few weeks.’ Nothing says residents held them for months.
Tempting. Employees and property taxes are both in the passage. But P3 says the certificates were ‘tendered by merchants.’ Right action, wrong party.
Wrong. The passage never says certificates went invalid for missing stamps, let alone most of them.
CORRECT. P3: ‘most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes.’
Opposite. The author’s point is that merchants did not pass scrip on; it went from employees to shopkeepers and back to the treasury.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: identify an assumption on which Kenning’s argument relies and cite evidence from her own work that tells against it
show that the stamp records on which Kenning bases her reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation are unreliable
clarify an ambiguity in Kenning’s use of the term “revival” that the second paragraph left unresolved
explain why Halvey’s council chose to make its scrip redeemable for town taxes
present a comparison between Halvey and another town that Kenning had too quickly dismissed
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens ‘Her argument also assumes that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did’ and then notes that ‘Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise,’ which is A. B is tempting because the paragraph draws on her figures, but it uses them rather than doubting them; the second paragraph even calls the reconstruction ingenious. C describes the second paragraph’s job and E the fourth’s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the third paragraph does in the author’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First two sentences of P3; compare the jobs of P2 and P4.

breakdown.analysis: Read the opening words: ‘Her argument also assumes…’ So P3 is the assumption criticism. Then: ‘Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise.’ The evidence against the assumption comes from her own data. The rest of the paragraph spells out what the scrip may really have been doing. Prephrase: name an assumption Kenning makes and use her own numbers against it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both halves check out: the assumption (merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents) and the counterevidence from ‘Kenning’s own figures.’
Tempting. P3 does lean on her figures. But it relies on them; it doesn’t say they’re unreliable. P2 calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious.’ The problem is her inference, not her records.
Wrong paragraph. The ‘revival’ ambiguity is P2’s criticism, and P3 never returns to it.
Wrong. P3 says what tax redemption let the scrip do in effect, but never explains why the council chose that design.
Wrong paragraph. The Corley comparison is P4.

questions.stem: In saying that the effect of the stamps “cannot be read directly from Halvey’s sales figures” (last paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: Halvey’s merchants did not keep reliable records of their sales while the scrip circulated
the stamps’ effect on spending was too small to appear in any record of sales
Halvey’s sales figures reflect influences other than the stamps and so do not by themselves show what the stamps contributed
the stamps increased the number of transactions in Halvey but had no effect on the total value of sales
sales figures measure the quantity of money in circulation rather than the speed at which it is spent
questions.explanation: The phrase sums up the three preceding paragraphs: the figures mix a possible rise in transaction counts with sales value, scrip may have worked through tax redemption, and a reopened mill could have contributed. So the figures cannot isolate the stamps’ contribution: C. D is the tempting trap because it echoes the second paragraph, but there the author says only that transactions ‘could’ rise while sales stagnated; and the same sentence of the last paragraph denies that the stamps were shown to be without effect. B similarly asserts a size of effect the author never estimates.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the author means by ‘cannot be read directly’ from the sales figures.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, read as a summary of P2–P4.

breakdown.analysis: Why can’t you just look at the sales numbers and see the stamps’ effect? Because P2–P4 gave three other things that could move those numbers: smaller split-up purchases, tax redemption doing the work, and a mill reopening. ‘Directly’ is the key word: the effect may be there, but it’s tangled with other causes. We need an answer that says: other factors are mixed in, so the figures alone don’t isolate the stamps.

choices.note: Wrong. The author never doubts the merchants’ records. The problem is interpretation, not record-keeping.
Too strong. The author doesn’t say the effect was small; P5 says only that it can’t be read off the figures. ‘Can’t be measured this way’ isn’t ‘too small to measure.’
CORRECT. The figures reflect several possible influences, so by themselves they don’t show the stamps’ share. That’s what ‘not directly’ means here.

Tempting. It’s the P2 scenario. But P2 says that ‘could’ happen, not that it did, and P5 opens with ‘None of this shows that the stamps were without effect.’ This states as fact what the author offered as a possibility.
Wrong. This mangles P2’s compliment about design versus quantity. The author never says sales figures measure the money supply.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help Kenning to answer the objection raised in the fourth paragraph?
choices: Corley’s scrip, like Halvey’s, could be used to pay property taxes owed to the town.
Corley’s merchants’ association recorded the total value of its members’ sales but not the number of their transactions.
Fewer of Corley’s merchants than of Halvey’s agreed to accept the scrip issued by their town.
Some other towns in the region that issued scrip with a stamp requirement saw no recovery in retail sales.
By the spring of 1933, Halvey’s retail sales had already risen nearly as far as they would rise during the entire period in which the scrip circulated.
questions.explanation: The objection is that Kenning cannot dismiss Corley because of its reopened railway shop when Halvey also had a reopened employer, a mill that resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. E shows that nearly all of Halvey’s recovery came before that reopening, so the mill cannot explain it, and the two towns are no longer parallel. B is tempting because it recalls the second paragraph’s transactions-versus-value point, but it bears on how Corley measured recovery, not on the alternative cause. A and C make Corley’s recovery look less due to stamps or scrip use, which if anything strengthens the objection; D weakens Kenning.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best rescues Kenning from the Corley objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4 in full, especially the last sentence (Halvey’s mill ‘resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933’); the timing in P1 (scrip from winter 1932, eighteen months).

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the objection. 1. Corley had no stamps and recovered just as fast. 2. Kenning says Corley’s recovery came from its reopened railway shop. 3. Author: fine, but Halvey had a reopened mill too, so maybe that explains Halvey’s recovery. So the objection lives on the Halvey mill. How does Kenning escape? Cut the mill off from Halvey’s recovery. If the recovery mostly happened before the mill reopened, the mill can’t be the cause, and Halvey is no longer like Corley. Prephrase: Halvey recovered before the mill came back. The right answer gives you that only through a date, so you have to connect ‘spring of 1933’ with ‘summer of 1933.’

choices.note: Wrong direction. If Corley’s scrip also redeemed for taxes, the two towns share the tax mechanism from P3 and differ only in the stamps. That makes Corley look like a fair test showing stamps weren’t needed, which hurts Kenning.

Tempting. It sounds like the P2 point about transactions versus total value, and it even suggests Corley’s figures measure value. But the fourth-paragraph objection is about an alternative cause (a reopened employer), and this does nothing about Halvey’s mill.

Wrong direction. If fewer Corley merchants took scrip yet Corley recovered just as fast, scrip (stamped or not) looks less important to recovery. That doesn’t help a stamps-explain-the-revival thesis.
Wrong direction. Stamped scrip with no recovery elsewhere is a point against Kenning, not a defense of her.

CORRECT. The mill resumed operation in the summer of 1933. If nearly all of Halvey’s rise had happened by spring, the mill can’t account for it, and the author’s ‘Halvey had a reopened employer too’ reply loses its force. Kenning’s distinction between the towns stands.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the second paragraph?
choices: Kenning’s figures show that the total value of Halvey’s retail sales stagnated while the scrip circulated.
A charge that makes holding money costly could increase the number of purchases without increasing the total amount spent.
Halvey’s merchants recorded the number of their transactions more accurately than the value of their sales.
Residents of Halvey generally preferred making small purchases to making large ones.
Kenning should have measured Halvey’s revival by the number of transactions rather than by the value of sales.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the number of transactions ‘could rise sharply even while total sales stagnated, if residents merely broke their purchases into smaller ones in order to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due,’ which is B stated generally. A is the tempting trap: it turns the author’s ‘could’ into a finding from Kenning’s figures. E takes a side the author never takes; the complaint is that Kenning wavers between the measures, not that she chose the wrong one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the second paragraph supports, without going beyond it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last two sentences of P2.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase exactly, but P2 makes one real claim: counting transactions and counting dollars can come apart. The stamp makes holding scrip costly, so people may split purchases to pass it on before the stamp is due. More transactions, same total spending. Watch for answers that turn ‘could’ into ‘did’ or pick a side on which measure is right.

choices.note: Tempting. It uses P2’s own words, but P2 says total sales ‘could’ stagnate while transactions rise. It never says Kenning’s figures show stagnation. A possibility isn’t a finding.
CORRECT. This is P2’s mechanism in general form: the stamp makes holding scrip costly, people split purchases, transactions go up, total spending may not.
We don’t know this. P2 says Kenning switches between the two measures, not that one was recorded more accurately.
Wrong. P2 says residents might split purchases to avoid the stamp, not that they liked small purchases. A reason forced by the stamp isn’t a preference.
Too far. The author’s complaint is that Kenning doesn’t clarify which she means. If anything, P2 suggests transaction counts are the weaker measure, since they can rise without more spending.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: The revival of Halvey’s retail trade was produced chiefly by the partial reopening of one of the town’s mills.
Kenning erred in relying on surviving stamp records to reconstruct the circulation of Halvey’s scrip.
Scrip that was redeemable for town taxes but carried no stamp requirement might have served Halvey’s council equally well as a means of paying its employees.
The experience of Corley demonstrates that the stamps had no effect on how quickly Halvey’s scrip was spent.
Historians of scrip should attend to the quantity of money issued rather than to the design of the currency.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the scrip may have functioned as a way for the town to pay employees out of future tax receipts, ‘a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce’; Corley’s stamp-free scrip and the last paragraph’s emphasis on the town’s ‘power to tax’ point the same way, so C. A and D are the tempting traps: the author says a reopened mill ‘could also have contributed’ and explicitly denies having shown that the stamps had no effect. B contradicts the praise of the reconstruction as ‘ingenious,’ and E reverses the credit given to Kenning for attending to design.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the author would accept, given the exact strength of the author’s claims.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of P3 (‘not one that the stamps were needed to produce’), P5, and the compliments at the start of P2.

breakdown.analysis: The author is careful. Notice what the author does and doesn’t commit to: 1. The stamps may have done something (P5: ‘None of this shows…’). 2. The mill ‘could’ have contributed, not ‘did.’ 3. The tax-receipt arrangement was useful and didn’t need the stamps (P3). So the safe answer is one built on point 3, hedged like the author. Prephrase: the town could have paid its workers with tax-redeemable scrip even without stamps.

choices.note: Tempting. The mill is the author’s best counterpoint to Kenning. But the author only says it ‘could also have contributed.’ ‘Chiefly produced’ is a commitment the author never makes. Too strong.
Opposite. The author calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious’ and uses Kenning’s own figures in P3. The records aren’t the problem.

CORRECT. P3: paying employees out of future tax receipts was ‘a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.’ A stamp-free, tax-redeemable scrip would give you that arrangement, and the hedge ‘might have’ matches the author’s caution.
Tempting. Corley is the author’s comparison case. But P5 says flat out, ‘None of this shows that the stamps were without effect.’ This puts in the author’s mouth exactly what the author disclaims.
Opposite. P2 credits Kenning for ‘attending to the design of a currency rather than merely to its quantity.’ The author likes that move.

questions.stimulus: Film critic: Many viewers assume that a remake exists only to cash in on the reputation of the original film. Some remakes surely do. But the new remake of the thriller Glass Harbor deserves to be watched on its own merits. Its director moved the story from a crowded city to a remote fishing village, and that change gives the familiar plot a sense of isolation the original never had. Admittedly, the remake’s dialogue is weaker than the original’s.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the film critic’s argument?
choices: Many remakes exist only to cash in on the reputation of the original film.
The remake of Glass Harbor has weaker dialogue than the original film has.
The remake of Glass Harbor is worth watching for its own qualities.
Moving a story to a new setting can give a familiar plot qualities the original lacked.
The remake of Glass Harbor is a better film than the original Glass Harbor.
questions.explanation: The critic grants that some remakes are cash-ins and that this one’s dialogue is weaker, but argues that the new setting makes the Glass Harbor remake worth watching on its own merits, which C restates. E is tempting, but the critic never ranks the remake above the original; a film can be worth watching without being better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new Glass Harbor remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its new fishing-village setting gives the plot an isolation the original lacked (support); some remakes are cash-ins and its dialogue is weaker (concessions).
