breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is a popular view, and 'Some remakes surely do' is a concession to it. 'But' flips to the critic's own view: this remake is worth watching for itself. The setting change is the reason given for that. The 'Admittedly' sentence is another concession. We need an answer that says the remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

choices.note: This is the popular view the critic pushes back on. The critic even grants that some remakes are like this, but that's a concession, not the point.
This is the 'Admittedly' concession. Concessions are things the author grants despite the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

CORRECT. 'Worth watching for its own qualities' is just a restatement of 'deserves to be watched on its own merits.' The setting change supports it; the other sentences are background and concessions.
Too general, and it's a premise. The critic says this particular setting change helped this particular film. That supports the conclusion; it isn't the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like a fan's verdict. But the critic never compares the films overall, and even admits the dialogue is worse. 'Worth watching' isn't 'better than the original.' Watch for unsupported rankings.

questions.stimulus: Nutrition blogger: The county health board urges residents to cut back on sugary drinks, pointing out that such drinks contribute to tooth decay and weight gain. Yet the vending machines in the health board’s own offices are stocked with soda, and board members have been seen drinking it at meetings. Clearly, then, residents can safely disregard the board’s advice.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the nutrition blogger’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: rejects a recommendation on the grounds that the people who make it do not act in accordance with it
takes for granted that anything that contributes to weight gain also contributes to tooth decay
fails to consider that residents might drink soda in moderation without suffering any harm
draws a conclusion about all of the board’s offices from what is stocked in only a few vending machines
takes for granted that residents trust the board less than they trust other sources of health advice
questions.explanation: The blogger dismisses the board’s health advice only because board members don’t follow it, which says nothing about whether sugary drinks actually cause decay and weight gain; A describes this. C is tempting because ‘safely’ sounds too strong, but the argument’s problem is not a failure to consider moderate drinking; it offers no evidence about the drinks at all.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Residents can safely ignore the health board’s advice to cut back on sugary drinks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The board’s own vending machines sell soda; board members drink soda at meetings.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the board members drink soda? Hypocrisy doesn't make the advice wrong. Sugar either contributes to tooth decay or it doesn't, no matter who's drinking it. This is ad hominem of the tu quoque type: dismissing an argument because its makers don't follow their own advice. It's a classic; know it. It's like a smoker telling his son not to smoke, and the son concluding smoking must be fine. We need an answer that says the blogger rejects the advice because of the advisers' behavior.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only reason given for ignoring the advice is that the board doesn't practice it. That's tu quoque, and it never touches whether the advice is true.
The blogger never links weight gain to tooth decay. The board simply names two effects.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since candy makes people gain weight, it must also rot their teeth.

choices.note: Tempting. 'Safely disregard' is strong, and moderation is a real issue. But the argument's flaw isn't missing the moderation point; it's that it gives no health evidence at all, only the board's behavior.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Doctors warn about soda, but one can a day is fine, so I'll keep drinking it. (ignoring that moderate use might be harmless)

choices.note: No sampling move here. The blogger isn't generalizing about all offices; the point is about the board's hypocrisy, which would be equally irrelevant if every machine sold soda.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Two vending machines at city hall sell soda, so every city office must sell soda.

choices.note: The blogger says nothing about how much residents trust the board or anyone else. The argument is about whether the advice can be ignored, not whom residents believe.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Residents will ignore the board's warning, since they surely trust their own doctors more.

questions.stimulus: Fisheries biologist: In the Merrow River, young salmon released from the hatchery survive to adulthood at a much lower rate than young salmon hatched in the wild. Hatchery salmon are fed by hand until their release and so have had little experience avoiding predators. Thus, the hatchery salmon’s lower survival rate is probably due largely to their inexperience with predators.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the fisheries biologist’s argument?
choices: Wild salmon in the Merrow River are, on average, slightly larger at a given age than hatchery salmon are.
The number of predatory fish in the Merrow River has risen over the past decade.
Some hatchery salmon survive to adulthood even though they were fed by hand before release.
Hatchery salmon that were briefly exposed to predatory fish in holding ponds before release survived at nearly the same rate as wild salmon.
Hatchery salmon are caught by anglers more often than wild salmon are, because anglers favor the stretch of river near the hatchery.
questions.explanation: If inexperience with predators is the cause, giving hatchery salmon some predator experience should close the survival gap, and D reports exactly that. E is tempting because it is about survival, but it supplies a different cause (anglers), which weakens rather than strengthens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive less well mainly because they lack experience avoiding predators.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive to adulthood less often than wild salmon; hatchery salmon are hand-fed and have little predator experience.

breakdown.analysis: Is predator inexperience really the cause? Hatchery fish differ from wild fish in lots of ways: size, genes, where they're released. To strengthen a causal claim, look for an answer that isolates the proposed cause: change only the predator experience and see whether survival changes. It's like testing whether a kid is failing math because he skips homework: make him do the homework and see whether his grades go up. We need an answer that says giving hatchery fish predator experience improves their survival.

choices.note: This points to a different difference between the groups: size. If anything it suggests another cause of the gap, so it doesn't help the biologist.
More predators would affect wild and hatchery salmon alike. It doesn't explain why one group survives worse than the other.
So? Some survivors in the hatchery group are expected even if the group does worse overall. This says nothing about why the rates differ.
CORRECT. This is the controlled test. Same hatchery fish, plus predator experience, and the survival gap nearly disappears. That points right at inexperience as the cause.
Tempting, because it's about why hatchery salmon die. But it names a different cause, anglers near the hatchery. That's an alternative explanation, so it weakens the argument.

questions.stimulus: School board chair: To save money, the district plans to eliminate the late bus that takes students home after evening activities such as play rehearsals and club meetings. But many students who stay for these activities have no other way to get home. So eliminating the late bus will reduce participation in evening activities.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the school board chair’s argument?
choices: The late bus costs the district more to operate than any other bus route does.
Not all of the students who have no other way home would keep staying for evening activities if the late bus were eliminated.
Evening activities are more valuable to students than the money saved by eliminating the late bus is to the district.
Most of the students who participate in evening activities have no other way to get home.
The district has no other way to save as much money as it would save by eliminating the late bus.
questions.explanation: The chair moves from ‘many participants have no other ride’ to ‘participation will fall,’ which requires that at least some of those students would actually stop staying; B says this modestly. D is too strong: the argument needs only that some participants would drop out, not that most participants lack a ride.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating the late bus will reduce participation in evening activities.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many students who stay for evening activities have no other way to get home.

breakdown.analysis: So what if they have no other ride? Would they actually stop coming? Maybe they'd walk, or stay anyway and figure it out. The argument needs at least some of these students to drop out of activities. We need an answer that says at least some of the students without another ride would stop staying for activities. Negation test: if every single one of them would keep staying, participation wouldn't drop, and the argument collapses.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The conclusion is about participation, not which route costs the most. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: The late bus does not cost more than every other route.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, every student without a ride keeps staying for activities anyway. Then nobody drops out and participation doesn't fall. The argument dies, so this is required.
choices.negation: All of the students who have no other way home would keep staying for evening activities if the late bus were eliminated.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The chair predicts what will happen to participation, not whether the cut is worth it. Negated, the prediction still stands.
choices.negation: Evening activities are not more valuable to students than the money saved is to the district.

choices.note: Too strong. The stimulus says 'many,' and the argument only needs some dropouts. Negated (only a minority lack a ride), participation can still fall.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most participating students have no other way home.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether there are other ways to save money bears on whether the cut is wise, not on whether participation will drop.
choices.negation: The district has some other way to save as much money.

questions.stimulus: Last year the regional airline Corran Air replaced the seats in its turboprop planes, which fly short mountain routes, with thinner, lighter seats. In surveys, passengers consistently rate the new seats as less comfortable than the old ones. Yet over the year after the change, Corran’s passenger satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Corran’s satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose?
choices: Corran’s competitors on the same mountain routes did not replace the seats in their planes.
Passengers on short flights care less about seat comfort than passengers on long flights do.
The new seats cost Corran less to buy and to maintain than the old seats did.
Satisfaction scores for Corran’s jet flights, whose seats were not replaced, did not change over the same year.
The lighter new seats mean that Corran’s turboprops now rarely have to leave checked bags behind to stay within weight limits.
questions.explanation: The lighter seats had a side benefit passengers notice: their bags now travel with them, which can outweigh a less comfortable seat on a short flight; E explains the rise. B is tempting, but caring less about comfort would at most keep scores from falling; it gives no reason for them to rise.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Corran put in seats passengers find less comfortable, but satisfaction with its turboprop flights went up.

breakdown.analysis: How does a worse seat lead to happier passengers? Look for something else the new seats did. Here the clue is in the stimulus: the seats are lighter, and the planes fly short mountain routes. Weight might matter. The defect (thin seats) could come bundled with a benefit. We need an answer that shows the change produced some gain passengers value more than seat comfort.

choices.note: So? What competitors did doesn't explain why Corran's own passengers became more satisfied with flights that got worse seats.
Tempting. It softens the blow of the worse seats. But 'cares less' only explains why scores might not drop much. It gives no reason for them to go up.
Wrong dimension. Savings to Corran explain why the airline made the change, not why passengers were happier.
This makes the puzzle sharper, not smaller. It rules out a general rise across the airline but provides no explanation for the turboprop increase.
CORRECT. The lighter seats mean bags stop getting left behind. Passengers hate losing their bags more than they mind a thinner seat on a short hop, so satisfaction rises.

questions.stimulus: Under Halbrook Insurance’s homeowner policy, a claim for water damage is paid only if the damage was reported within thirty days. Moreover, any claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe is paid in full, provided that the damage was reported within thirty days and the home’s pipes had been professionally inspected within the preceding five years. The Delgado family’s claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe was paid, but not in full.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The Delgados reported the water damage more than thirty days after it occurred.
Halbrook pays in full only claims for water damage caused by burst pipes.
The Delgados’ pipes had not been professionally inspected within the five years before the damage.
Some claims for water damage not caused by burst pipes are paid in full by Halbrook.
Halbrook would have refused the Delgados’ claim entirely if their pipes had not been inspected within the preceding five years.
questions.explanation: Because the claim was paid at all, the damage was reported within thirty days; it was a burst pipe; so if the pipes had been inspected within five years it would have been paid in full. It wasn’t, so the inspection condition failed, as C says. A is the reversal trap: being paid proves the report was timely.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Water claim paid → reported within 30 days; 2. Burst pipe AND reported within 30 days AND inspected within 5 years → paid in full; 3. Delgados: burst pipe, claim paid, not in full.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Paid → reported within 30 days. So the Delgados reported on time. They had a burst pipe. Rule 2: burst pipe + on time + inspected → paid in full. Contrapositive: not paid in full → not burst pipe OR not on time OR not inspected. They had a burst pipe and reported on time, so the only condition left to fail is the inspection. We need: the pipes weren't inspected within five years.

choices.note: This reverses the facts. The claim was paid, and payment requires a report within thirty days. So they must have reported on time.
We don't know this. The policy gives one route to full payment; it never says burst pipes are the only route.
CORRECT. Burst pipe and an on-time report (proven by payment) plus an inspection would have guaranteed full payment. They didn't get full payment, so the inspection piece is missing.
We don't know this. The policy says nothing about full payment for other kinds of water damage. Could be true; doesn't have to be.
Contradicted. Their pipes weren't inspected, and their claim was still paid in part. So lacking an inspection doesn't mean total refusal.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: At the ancient settlement of Kerrin, many houses had a shallow, stone-lined pit set into the floor just inside the doorway. Similar stone-lined pits found in houses in other regions of the same era were used for storing grain. So the pits at Kerrin were probably used to store grain as well.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologist’s argument?
choices: The pits at Kerrin contain thick layers of ash and burned animal bone, and no grain residue has been found in any of them.
Grain was grown in fields surrounding Kerrin during the period when the houses were occupied.
Some of the houses at Kerrin did not have a stone-lined pit near the doorway.
Storage pits in some other regions were lined with clay rather than with stone.
The people of Kerrin traded regularly with people living in regions where pits were used for storing grain.
questions.explanation: The argument guesses the pits’ function from their resemblance to grain pits elsewhere; A gives direct evidence of a different use (fires or cooking) and no sign of grain. B and E are tempting only because they mention grain and the other regions, but both make grain storage more plausible, not less.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The pits at Kerrin were probably used for storing grain.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Similar stone-lined pits in other regions of the same era stored grain.

breakdown.analysis: Looking alike doesn't mean being used alike. A pit is a pit; it could hold grain, coals, water, or trash. This is a function guess based on analogy, and the classic way to weaken it is with evidence of a different function. We need an answer showing the Kerrin pits were used for something other than grain.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ash and burned bone suggest a hearth or cooking pit, and no grain residue anywhere is a bad sign for a granary. This points to a different function.
This makes grain storage more likely, not less. People who grow grain need somewhere to store it.
Irrelevant. The argument is about the houses that had pits. Some houses lacking one doesn't tell us what the pits were for.
So? The Kerrin pits are stone-lined like the grain pits the archaeologist compares them to. Clay-lined pits elsewhere don't weaken that match.
This strengthens the analogy. Trade contact makes it more likely that Kerrin shared practices with the grain-storing regions.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: In a recent study, 200 adults fluent in both Spanish and English were asked to describe a dream they had had in the past week. Seventy percent of them switched between their two languages at least once while doing so. This shows that recounting dreams tends to bring out language switching in bilingual people.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the linguist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the participants were equally fluent in both of their languages
draws a conclusion about bilingual people in general from a sample that is too small to be meaningful
takes for granted that people remember the details of their recent dreams accurately
confuses a possible cause of language switching with an effect of language switching
fails to establish how often bilingual adults switch languages when describing experiences other than dreams
questions.explanation: To show that dreams in particular bring out switching, the linguist needs a baseline: if these speakers switch just as often describing their commute, the dream topic did nothing. E names the missing comparison. B is tempting, but 200 participants is not obviously too few, and even a huge sample would not fix the lack of a baseline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recounting dreams tends to bring out language switching in bilinguals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of 200 bilingual adults switched languages at least once while describing a recent dream.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent switched. Compared to what? Maybe these people switch languages constantly, whatever they're talking about. If 70 percent also switch while describing yesterday's lunch, dreams have nothing special to do with it. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw: the study measured only one condition. It's like noting that 90 percent of people drink water at a concert and deciding concerts make people thirsty. We need an answer that points out the missing baseline: how often they switch when describing other things.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need equal fluency. Unequal fluency might affect switching in general, but it doesn't touch the jump to 'dreams cause it.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: These bilinguals switch rarely, so switching must be hard for everyone who speaks two languages. (assumes equal skill in both)

choices.note: Tempting. Sample complaints are a common right answer. But 200 people isn't obviously tiny, and the real problem would remain even with 20,000: no comparison to non-dream talk.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Three bilingual friends of mine never switch languages, so bilinguals rarely switch.

choices.note: Accuracy of the dream content doesn't matter. The study is about how people talk, not whether their dream reports are true.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Participants said they dreamed about flying, so most people dream about flying.

choices.note: No cause/effect reversal here. Nobody suggests switching languages causes people to recount dreams.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: People who switch languages tell more stories, so telling stories must make people switch.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without a baseline for switching during other descriptions, the 70 percent figure can't show that dreams in particular bring switching out.

questions.stimulus: In the Tavish language, a word borrowed from another language keeps its original stress pattern for at least a generation after it enters Tavish. Every native Tavish word is stressed on its first syllable. The common Tavish word ‘kelmaro’ is stressed on its second syllable.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: ‘Kelmaro’ entered Tavish within the past generation.
‘Kelmaro’ is not a native Tavish word.
Most words borrowed into Tavish are stressed on their second syllable.
Borrowed words that have been in Tavish for more than a generation are stressed on their first syllable.
‘Kelmaro’ was borrowed from a language in which it was stressed on its second syllable.
questions.explanation: Native words are always stressed on the first syllable; ‘kelmaro’ is not, so it cannot be native, as B says. A and D misread ‘at least a generation’: borrowed words keep their stress for a generation or longer, so a word stressed on its second syllable may have been borrowed long ago, and nothing says older borrowings shift.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Borrowed word → keeps original stress for at least a generation; 2. Native Tavish word → stressed on first syllable; 3. ‘Kelmaro’ is stressed on its second syllable.

breakdown.analysis: Start with the cleanest rule. Native → first-syllable stress. Contrapositive: not first-syllable stress → not native. Kelmaro is stressed on the second syllable, so it isn't native. Done. Watch the phrase 'at least a generation.' It sets a minimum, not a maximum. It doesn't say what happens after a generation, so answers about timing or later stress changes are unsupported.

choices.note: Tempting. It feels like a borrowed word that still has odd stress must be recent. But 'at least a generation' means borrowed words may keep their stress much longer. Kelmaro could be centuries old.
CORRECT. Native words are always first-syllable stressed. Kelmaro isn't, so it isn't native. This one actually must be true.
We don't know this. One second-syllable word tells us nothing about most borrowed words.
Reads a maximum into a minimum. The stimulus never says borrowed words shift after a generation; they keep their stress for at least that long, maybe forever.

We don't know this. Kelmaro isn't native, but if it was borrowed long ago its stress could have shifted, and it might not even be borrowed (it could, for example, have been formed some other way). Its original stress is unknown.

questions.stimulus: School board member: The district’s cafeteria vendor has proposed adding flavored milk to the lunch menu, noting that students would drink more milk if it were offered. Flavored milk does supply calcium, which growing children need. But it also contains a considerable amount of added sugar, and many parents have told the board they do not want their children offered sugary drinks at school. So we should decline the vendor’s proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the school board member’s reasoning?
choices: A school should offer students whatever nutritious foods they are most likely to consume, regardless of any other concerns.
Decisions about school menus should be based solely on nutritional considerations, not on the preferences of parents.
A food that supplies a nutrient children need should be offered at school even if it contains added sugar.
A school should not offer a food that many parents object to on health grounds, even if the food has some nutritional value.
A school should accept a vendor’s proposal only if the vendor can show that students would benefit from it.
questions.explanation: The member concedes that flavored milk has a nutritional benefit but declines it because many parents object to sugary drinks; D says exactly that parental health objections override some nutritional value. E is tempting, but the vendor arguably did show a benefit (more milk, more calcium), so E would not tell the board to decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board should decline the proposal to add flavored milk.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Flavored milk supplies calcium (concession) but has added sugar; many parents don't want sugary drinks offered to their children at school.

breakdown.analysis: Why say no to milk that kids would actually drink? Because of the sugar and the parents' objections, even granting the calcium. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: decline. And it should fit the reasons: parent objections on health grounds beat a nutritional upside. We need a rule like: when many parents object to a food for health reasons, don't offer it, even if it has some benefit.

choices.note: This points the other way. Students would drink more flavored milk, and it's nutritious in part, so this rule supports offering it.
This throws out the parents' objections, which are the heart of the member's reasoning. It doesn't lead to declining.
Opposite. This would tell the board to offer flavored milk, since it supplies calcium.

CORRECT. Many parents object on health grounds (sugar), and the rule says don't offer the food even though it has some nutritional value (calcium). Every piece of the argument is covered, and the rule tells the board to decline.
Tempting. It sounds cautious. But the vendor pointed to a benefit, more milk and so more calcium, so this rule might even favor accepting. It doesn't use the sugar or the parents at all.

questions.stimulus: Airline spokesperson: Since Daventry Air adopted its new maintenance program two years ago, our pilots have reported 30 percent fewer in-flight mechanical malfunctions per thousand flights than they did before. Clearly, the new program has made Daventry’s flights safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson’s argument?
choices: Since the new program was adopted, Daventry’s flights have become longer, on average, than they were before.
Other airlines that adopted maintenance programs similar to Daventry’s also saw declines in the number of reported in-flight malfunctions.
Under the new program, engine and flight-control malfunctions have become more frequent, while malfunctions of cabin items such as coffee makers have declined sharply.
The new maintenance program costs Daventry considerably more each year than its previous program did.
Both before and after the new program was adopted, some Daventry pilots failed to report minor malfunctions.
questions.explanation: The argument measures safety by the number of malfunctions, but safety depends on which malfunctions occur; C shows the dangerous ones rose while trivial ones fell, so fewer total malfunctions does not mean safer flights. E is tempting, but underreporting that happened both before and after does not explain the change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new maintenance program has made Daventry’s flights safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reported in-flight malfunctions per thousand flights fell 30 percent after the program began.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of malfunctions really the measure of safety? A broken coffee maker and a failing engine each count as one malfunction. If the small stuff went down and the serious stuff went up, the total drops while flights get more dangerous. This is a count-versus-severity mismatch. We need an answer that says the decline came from trivial malfunctions while dangerous ones didn't fall (or rose).

choices.note: Longer flights give more chances for something to break per flight. If malfunctions still fell, that makes the program look even better. Not a weakener.
This strengthens. If similar programs elsewhere also cut malfunctions, the program likely did something here too.
CORRECT. The total fell because cabin gadgets broke less, but engine and flight-control problems, the ones that matter for safety, became more common. Fewer malfunctions, less safety.
Wrong dimension. Cost has nothing to do with whether flights are safer.
Tempting, because underreporting can distort numbers. But it happened both before and after, so it can't explain the drop. A constant problem doesn't create a change.

questions.stimulus: Film critic: Some critics hold that a film should be judged a failure if most viewers leave the theater confused about its plot. But by that standard, several films now universally regarded as masterpieces would have to be counted as failures, since their plots baffled nearly everyone who saw them on their first release. Clearly, then, confusing most viewers is not by itself enough to make a film a failure.
questions.stem: The claim that several films now universally regarded as masterpieces would have to be counted as failures plays which one of the following roles in the film critic’s argument?
choices: It is the conclusion that the critic’s argument is intended to establish.
It is a consequence of a proposed standard that the critic presents as a reason to reject that standard.
It is a premise offered by some critics in support of the standard they propose.
It is a claim that the critic concedes is true but argues is irrelevant to judging films.
It is an example offered to show that most viewers misjudge films the first time they see them.
questions.explanation: The critic derives this result from the other critics’ standard and treats it as absurd, which is why the standard must be rejected; B describes that role. A is wrong because the conclusion is the final sentence, that confusion alone doesn’t make a film a failure; this claim supports it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Confusing most viewers is not by itself enough to make a film a failure.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If confusion made a film a failure, several acknowledged masterpieces that baffled their first audiences would count as failures.

breakdown.analysis: The critic doesn't believe the masterpieces are failures. It's the absurd result used to sink the rule. This is the classic hypothetical-consequence move: take someone's standard, show it leads somewhere ridiculous, and reject the standard. We need an answer that says the claim is a consequence of the other critics' standard, offered as grounds for rejecting it.

choices.note: The conclusion is the last sentence. This claim is the reason for it, not the point itself.
CORRECT. 'By that standard ... would have to be counted as failures' is the consequence of the other critics' rule, and the critic uses its absurdity to reject the rule.
Opposite side. The other critics would never offer this; it undercuts their standard. The film critic raises it against them.
The critic doesn't concede it's true. The whole point is that masterpieces are not failures. And it's highly relevant, not irrelevant.
Tempting, since first audiences were confused. But the claim isn't about viewers misjudging films. It's about what the standard would imply.

questions.stimulus: Fisheries economist: Three years ago, the Pell Bay fisheries authority shortened the crab-fishing season from six months to four. Since then, the average yearly income of Pell Bay’s crab fishers has fallen by a fifth. Therefore, the shortened season has reduced the incomes of the bay’s crab fishers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the fisheries economist’s argument?
choices: Crab fishers in Pell Bay earn most of their income from crab rather than from other catches.
The crab population in Pell Bay has not grown since the season was shortened.
The authority shortened the season mainly to protect the bay’s crab population.
The price that crab fishers receive for their catch has not fallen at all during the past three years.
Had the season stayed six months long, the fishers’ average income would not have fallen just as much.
questions.explanation: To blame the shorter season, the economist must assume the income drop would not have happened anyway; E states that counterfactual, and negating it (incomes would have fallen just as much regardless) destroys the argument. D is the attractive trap: a price drop would be an alternative cause, but the argument doesn’t need prices to have stayed perfectly flat, since a small price drop could coexist with the season cut doing real harm.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The shortened season reduced crab fishers’ incomes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The season was cut from six months to four; average income has since fallen by a fifth.

breakdown.analysis: Income fell after the season was shortened. Would it have fallen anyway? Maybe prices crashed or fuel costs soared. To blame a policy, you have to assume the outcome wouldn't have happened without it. It's like blaming a new coach for a losing season when the star player also retired. We need an answer that says incomes wouldn't have dropped as much if the season had stayed six months. Negate each choice and see which one kills the argument.

choices.note: Not required. Even if crab is only part of their income, a shorter crab season can still reduce what they earn. Negating it leaves the argument standing.
choices.negation: Crab fishers in Pell Bay do not earn most of their income from crab.

choices.note: Not required. If the crab population grew, fishers might catch more per day, which if anything makes the income drop more likely due to the season. The negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The crab population in Pell Bay has grown since the season was shortened.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Why the authority acted has nothing to do with whether the change cut incomes.
choices.negation: The authority did not shorten the season mainly to protect the crab population.

choices.note: Tempting. A price drop is a possible alternative cause. But 'not fallen at all' is too strong. Negated, prices dipped a little, and the season cut could still have done most of the damage. The argument survives.
choices.negation: The price crab fishers receive has fallen somewhat during the past three years.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, incomes would have fallen just as much with a six-month season. Then the shorter season made no difference, and the conclusion collapses. This is the counterfactual every 'the policy caused it' argument needs.
choices.negation: Had the season stayed six months long, the fishers’ average income would have fallen just as much.

questions.stimulus: Every film in the Lindqvist retrospective was shot on 70-millimeter film. A 70-millimeter film can be projected at the Orlov Cinema only if the cinema’s old wide-gauge projector is repaired. So unless that projector is repaired, none of the films in the Lindqvist retrospective can be projected at the Orlov Cinema.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: All of the cars in Mira’s delivery fleet run on diesel. A diesel car may enter the city center on weekdays only if the city lifts its emissions ban. So unless the city lifts the ban, none of the cars in Mira’s fleet may enter the city center on weekdays.

Every exhibit at the Corso Gallery that requires dim lighting is a textile. The gallery can display textiles only if its humidity system is working. So if the humidity system is working, all of the dim-lit exhibits can be displayed.
Every runner on the team trains on the school track. The track can be used only if it has been resurfaced. The track has been resurfaced. So every runner on the team can use the track.

Some of the songs on the new album were recorded in Studio 4. A song recorded in Studio 4 can be released only if the studio’s owner consents. So unless the owner consents, none of the songs on the album can be released.
Every apartment in the Marlow Building has a gas stove. A gas stove can be installed only by a licensed fitter. So every licensed fitter in the city has installed a stove in the Marlow Building.
questions.explanation: The original is valid: all A are B; a B can do C only if D; so without D, no A can do C. A matches each step. D is the closest trap, but it starts from ‘some’ songs, so its ‘none of the songs’ conclusion does not follow, and B and C treat the necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless the projector is repaired, none of the retrospective’s films can be projected at the Orlov.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every retrospective film is 70 mm; a 70 mm film can be projected there only if the projector is repaired.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; a B can do C only if D; so if not D, no A can do C. (A → B → (C requires D); not D → no A does C.)

breakdown.analysis: Map it out. Retrospective film → 70 mm. 70 mm projected → projector repaired. Contrapositive: not repaired → no 70 mm film projected → no retrospective film projected. It's a valid chain with an 'all' starting group and a necessary condition. We need an answer with: an 'all' group, a necessary condition ('only if') for that group's members, and a conclusion that without the condition, none of the group can do the thing.

choices.note: CORRECT. All fleet cars → diesel; diesel enters on weekdays → ban lifted; so no ban lift → no fleet car enters. Same quantifier, same 'only if,' same 'unless ... none' conclusion.
This treats the necessary condition as sufficient. The humidity system working is required for display, but the argument concludes that it guarantees display. The original never does that.

Also turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one: resurfacing is required for use, but that doesn't mean every runner can use the track once it's resurfaced. It also asserts the condition is met, unlike the original.

Tempting, because the conclusion is worded almost identically. But it starts with 'some' songs. The other songs might not need the owner's consent, so 'none can be released' doesn't follow. The original starts with 'every.'
This reverses the relationship. From 'stoves require licensed fitters,' it concludes every fitter installed a stove there. Nothing like the original's structure.

questions.stimulus: School board member: Five years ago, our district ranked third among the state’s forty school districts in average reading scores on the statewide exam. This year, among those same forty districts, it ranked eleventh. Clearly, our students are reading less well than our students did five years ago, and we need to overhaul the reading curriculum.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the school board member’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that the other districts in the state use the same reading curriculum as the board member’s district does
fails to consider the possibility that new districts were added to the state’s rankings over the five years
draws a conclusion about all of the district’s students from the exam scores of only some of them
treats a decline in the district’s standing relative to other districts as though it established a decline in the district’s own performance
infers that the district’s scores will keep falling from the fact that its ranking has fallen over a five-year period
questions.explanation: A drop from third to eleventh is consistent with the district’s own scores rising, so long as eight districts improved even more; the argument treats a fall in rank as a fall in absolute reading ability, as D says. B is tempting but is ruled out by the stimulus, which compares the same forty districts, and E attributes a prediction the board member never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The district’s students read less well than its students did five years ago (so the curriculum needs an overhaul).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The district fell from third to eleventh among the same forty districts in average reading scores.

breakdown.analysis: Falling in the rankings doesn't mean getting worse. Imagine the district's average went from 70 to 75 while eight other districts jumped from the 60s to the 80s. The district is reading better and still drops to eleventh. This is the ranking-to-absolute flaw: a relative position treated as an absolute level. Watch the switch from a relative measure (rank) to an absolute claim (reading less well). We need an answer that says the argument treats a drop in relative standing as a drop in actual performance.

choices.note: The argument assumes nothing about other districts' curricula. Rank comparisons don't require shared curricula.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our district outscores Harlan, so our curriculum must be better than Harlan's curriculum. (assumes the difference is due to curriculum)

choices.note: Tempting, because new entrants could push a district down. But the stimulus says 'among those same forty districts,' so this possibility is already ruled out.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We were third of ten last year and fifth of thirty this year, so we've gotten worse.

choices.note: Nothing suggests only some students' scores were used; it's the district's average. And sampling isn't the problem here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The honors class read well, so all of our students read well.

choices.note: CORRECT. Eleventh instead of third only means more districts are ahead now. The district's own scores could have gone up. Relative rank isn't absolute performance.
The board member never predicts future scores. The conclusion is about now versus five years ago, plus a recommendation.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our scores fell this year, so they'll keep falling next year.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Any pottery fragment that bears traces of lead glaze was made after the end of the Varn period, since potters in this region learned lead glazing only from traders who arrived at the very end of that period. The pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of the dig at Osk Hill bear traces of lead glaze. Therefore, the lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period ended.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the archaeologist’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every pottery fragment made after the Varn period bears traces of lead glaze.
Any layer at a dig that contains pottery fragments made after the Varn period was deposited after the Varn period ended.
The traders who introduced lead glazing to the region settled at Osk Hill.
Pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of a dig are usually the oldest fragments at that dig.
No pottery made during the Varn period has been found at Osk Hill.
questions.explanation: The premises establish only that the lowest layer’s fragments were made after the Varn period; B links fragments to the layer, so the layer’s date follows. A reverses the conditional about glaze, and D says only what is usually true of lowest layers, so neither guarantees the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lead-glazed fragment → made after the Varn period; the lowest layer’s fragments are lead-glazed.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what we have: lowest-layer fragments → lead-glazed → made after Varn. But the conclusion is about when the layer was deposited, not when the pottery was made. Could fragments made later get into an older layer? Burrowing animals, later digging. The missing link is: layer contains post-Varn fragments → layer deposited post-Varn. Full chain: lowest-layer fragments → glazed → made after Varn → (assumption) layer deposited after Varn. We need that bridge from the fragments' date to the layer's date.

choices.note: This reverses the conditional. We already know glazed → after Varn. Knowing after Varn → glazed adds nothing about when the layer was deposited.
CORRECT. The lowest layer contains fragments made after Varn, and this rule says any such layer was deposited after Varn. The conclusion follows exactly.
Irrelevant. Where the traders lived doesn't connect the fragments' date to the layer's date.
Tempting, since it's about the lowest layer. But 'usually the oldest' doesn't tell us the layer was laid down after the fragments were made, and 'usually' can't guarantee anything.
So? Finding no Varn-period pottery doesn't show when the lowest layer was deposited. The layer could still predate the glazed fragments that ended up in it.

questions.stimulus: Insurance analyst: Kestrel Mutual offers its auto-insurance customers an optional dashboard monitor that beeps whenever the driver brakes harshly or accelerates sharply. Last year, Kestrel drivers who had installed the monitor filed 25 percent fewer accident claims than Kestrel drivers who had not. So using the monitor makes people drive more safely.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the insurance analyst’s argument?
choices: How much does Kestrel Mutual charge its customers for the dashboard monitor?
Do any other auto insurers offer their customers a monitor similar to Kestrel’s?
Are claims for accidents more costly for Kestrel to pay than other kinds of claims are?
Did Kestrel drivers without the monitor file more accident claims last year than in previous years?
Before installing the monitor, did the drivers who chose to install it file fewer accident claims than other Kestrel drivers did?
questions.explanation: Drivers chose to install the monitor, so they may simply have been safer drivers to begin with; whether they already filed fewer claims before installing it decides whether the monitor deserves the credit, which is why E is useful. D is tempting, but last year’s comparison between the two groups is unaffected by whether the non-monitor group did better or worse than in earlier years.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Using the monitor makes people drive more safely.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, Kestrel drivers with the optional monitor filed 25 percent fewer accident claims than those without.

breakdown.analysis: Who installs an optional safety beeper? Probably careful drivers. If the monitor group was already safer before getting it, the monitor didn't cause the difference; the type of driver did. This is a self-selected group. An evaluate question wants a question whose answer cuts both ways: one answer helps, the other hurts. We need a question about whether the monitor users were already safer before they installed it.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Price doesn't tell us whether the monitor changes driving. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.
Irrelevant. Other insurers' products don't affect whether Kestrel's monitor makes its drivers safer.
Irrelevant. Cost to Kestrel of a claim says nothing about whether the monitor reduces accidents.

Tempting, because it involves a before-and-after comparison. But the argument compares the two groups last year. Whether the no-monitor group got worse or better over time doesn't explain the gap between groups.
CORRECT. If yes, the monitor users were already safer drivers, and self-selection, not the monitor, explains the gap. If no, the monitor looks like the real cause. Either answer matters.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: It is often said that text messaging is eroding young people’s ability to spell, since their messages are full of abbreviations such as ‘thx’ and ‘l8r.’ But to shorten a word deliberately in such ways, a writer must know how the full word is normally spelled and how it sounds. And studies find that the students who use such abbreviations most often tend to score at least as well on spelling tests as students who rarely use them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the linguist’s argument?
choices: students who send many text messages will gradually lose the ability to spell common words correctly
frequent text messaging improves young people’s ability to spell
a young person’s frequent use of texting abbreviations is not, by itself, a sign of weak spelling ability
students who rarely send text messages tend to score poorly on spelling tests
abbreviations in text messages are harder to produce than the conventionally spelled words they replace
questions.explanation: The linguist pushes back on the popular view by arguing that abbreviating requires knowing the spelling and that heavy abbreviators spell at least as well as others; the modest conclusion that abbreviating is not itself a sign of poor spelling, C, follows. B is the attractive overreach: the evidence shows no deficit, not that texting causes improvement.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: texting abbreviations erode spelling; 2. Deliberate abbreviating requires knowing the normal spelling and sound; 3. Heavy abbreviators score at least as well on spelling tests as light users.

breakdown.analysis: The 'But' tells you the linguist is pushing back on the popular view, so the blank should reject or undercut it, not repeat it. How far can we go? The evidence shows abbreviators know spelling and do no worse. That knocks out 'abbreviations show bad spelling.' It does not show texting makes spelling better: 'at least as well' isn't 'better,' and a correlation can't prove a cause. We need a modest answer: using these abbreviations doesn't by itself indicate poor spelling.

choices.note: This is the popular view the linguist is arguing against. A completion that repeats the opponent's claim after a 'But' is backwards.

Tempting, because it's the opposite of the popular view. But the evidence is only that heavy texters do no worse, 'at least as well.' That's not improvement, and a correlation can't show texting causes anything. Polar opposite isn't the logical opposite.

CORRECT. Abbreviating requires knowing the spelling, and heavy abbreviators spell at least as well as others. So abbreviation use alone isn't evidence of weak spelling. It's exactly as strong as the evidence allows.
We don't know this. Heavy users score at least as well as rare users; that doesn't mean rare users score poorly. Both groups might score well.
Unsupported comparison. Abbreviating requires knowing the full word, but nothing says it's harder than writing the full word.

questions.stimulus: At Hollin Regional Airport, every flight that departs after 10 p.m. is operated by either Skylark Airways or Tern Air. All of Skylark’s flights from Hollin depart before 9 p.m. Every Tern Air flight from Hollin departs from Gate 4.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: A flight departs from Hollin after 10 p.m. from a gate other than Gate 4.
Some flights that depart from Gate 4 are operated by airlines other than Tern Air.
No Tern Air flight departs from Hollin after 10 p.m.
Some Skylark flights depart from Gate 4.
Every flight that departs from Hollin’s Gate 4 departs after 10 p.m.
questions.explanation: A flight after 10 p.m. must be Skylark or Tern; it can’t be Skylark, whose flights all leave before 9 p.m.; so it is Tern and leaves from Gate 4. A contradicts that chain. C is tempting, but nothing says any flight departs after 10 p.m., so Tern might have no late flights.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Departs after 10 p.m. → Skylark or Tern; 2. Skylark → departs before 9 p.m.; 3. Tern → Gate 4.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. After 10 p.m. → Skylark or Tern. Skylark flights leave before 9, so a flight after 10 can't be Skylark. So: after 10 p.m. → Tern → Gate 4. Any flight after 10 leaves from Gate 4. Now look for the answer that breaks this. Remember, the rules go one way: Gate 4 doesn't have to mean Tern, and Tern doesn't have to mean late.

choices.note: CORRECT. A post-10 p.m. flight must be Tern (Skylark is ruled out by its schedule), and every Tern flight uses Gate 4. A late flight from another gate is impossible.
Could be true. Tern → Gate 4 doesn't mean Gate 4 → Tern. Other airlines can share the gate.
Tempting, because Tern seems like 'the late airline.' But the rules never say any flight leaves after 10 p.m. If none do, this is true.
Could be true. Nothing restricts Skylark's gates. A Skylark flight could leave from Gate 4 at 7 p.m.
Could be true. If only Tern uses Gate 4 and all Tern flights leave after 10, every Gate 4 flight is late. Nothing rules that out.

questions.stimulus: Westbury school district policy: A student may be excused from the physical education requirement only if a parent or guardian submits a written request for the exemption, and only if either the student has a physician’s note documenting a medical condition that makes participation unsafe or the student is a member of a school-sponsored sports team that practices at least four days a week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: Lena’s mother submitted a written request, and Lena plays on the school’s volleyball team, which practices five days a week. So Lena must be excused from the physical education requirement.
Omar has a physician’s note documenting that his asthma makes participation unsafe, though no written request has been submitted for him. Since his need is documented, Omar may be excused.
Priya’s father submitted a written request, and Priya swims on a private club team that trains six days a week. So Priya may be excused from the physical education requirement.
Theo’s guardian submitted a written request, but Theo has no physician’s note, and the school’s cross-country team, on which he runs, practices only three days a week. So Theo may not be excused.
Mira has a physician’s note documenting a knee injury that makes participation unsafe, and her mother submitted a written request. But because Mira is not on any school team, she may not be excused.
questions.explanation: The policy states only necessary conditions: a written request, plus either a physician’s note or a school team practicing four or more days a week. Theo has neither a note nor a qualifying team, so the policy rules out excusing him, as D says. A is the attractive trap: Lena meets every necessary condition, but the policy never says meeting them guarantees an exemption, so ‘must be excused’ does not follow.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Excused → (written request) AND (physician’s note OR school-sponsored team practicing 4+ days a week).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment the policy actually supports. Since the policy lists only requirements, it can prove a student may NOT be excused (a requirement fails), but it can never prove a student must or may be excused.

breakdown.analysis: Read 'only if' carefully. Both conditions are necessary, not sufficient. Contrapositive: no written request → not excused; no note AND no qualifying team → not excused. So the safest conforming judgment denies an exemption to someone who fails a requirement. Check each student: Does a request exist? Is there a note, or a school team with 4+ practice days? A right answer must show a student failing one of those and conclude 'may not be excused.'

choices.note: Tempting. Lena meets every requirement: request, school team, five days. But meeting necessary conditions doesn't guarantee anything. The policy never says who must be excused. 'Must' goes too far.
Omar fails the written-request requirement. The policy says no request → not excused, so concluding he may be excused contradicts it.
Priya's team is a private club, not school-sponsored, and she has no note. She fails the 'either' condition, so the policy points toward denying her, not excusing her.
CORRECT. Theo has the request, but no note, and his school team practices only three days. He fails the 'either ... or' requirement, so under the policy he may not be excused.

Mira satisfies the 'or' through her physician's note; she doesn't also need a team. Denying her because she's not on a team misreads 'either ... or' as 'both.' The policy gives no ground for that denial.

questions.stimulus: Public health researcher: Two years ago, the city of Ostrel imposed a tax on sweetened beverages. Since then, sales of sweetened beverages in Ostrel’s stores have fallen by 30 percent, while sales in stores in the neighboring city of Varda, which has no such tax, have remained unchanged. So the tax has substantially reduced the amount of sweetened beverages that Ostrel residents consume.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researcher’s argument?
choices: Since the tax took effect, sales of unsweetened bottled water in Ostrel’s stores have risen.
Most of the stores in Ostrel that sell sweetened beverages opposed the tax when it was proposed.
Before the tax took effect, Ostrel residents bought considerably more sweetened beverages per person than Varda residents did.
Sales of sweetened beverages at Ostrel’s restaurants, which also must pay the tax, have declined since the tax took effect.
Since the tax began, sweetened-beverage sales have risen at Varda stores just across the border from Ostrel but fallen about as much at Varda’s other stores.
questions.explanation: E shows that Varda’s ‘unchanged’ total hides two things: a jump at border stores (suggesting Ostrel residents are crossing over to buy untaxed drinks) and a decline elsewhere (suggesting a regional drop unrelated to the tax), so Ostrel’s store sales overstate any fall in residents’ consumption caused by the tax. D is the trap: it is about Ostrel and the tax, but a drop in restaurant sales too makes a real fall in consumption more likely, so it strengthens rather than weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tax substantially reduced how much sweetened beverage Ostrel residents consume.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ostrel store sales fell 30 percent after the tax; store sales in untaxed Varda stayed the same.

breakdown.analysis: Two questions. First, are store sales in Ostrel the same as what Ostrel residents drink? Not if they buy elsewhere. Second, is Varda a clean comparison? 'Unchanged' is a total, and totals can hide offsetting moves. The strongest weakener would hit both: show residents buying across the border and show that the comparison city's flat total masks a downturn. Hard to prephrase exactly; look for an answer that breaks the link between Ostrel store sales and Ostrel consumption, or that breaks the Varda comparison.

choices.note: This strengthens. People switching to water is just what you'd expect if the tax really cut their sweetened-drink consumption.
Irrelevant. Store owners' opinions about the tax say nothing about what residents now drink.
Tempting, because a high starting point leaves room to fall. But that doesn't explain why Ostrel fell and Varda didn't, or suggest the tax wasn't responsible.

Tempting, because it’s about the tax and another place Ostrel residents buy drinks. But read the direction: restaurant sales fell too, so residents didn’t just move their purchases to restaurants. That supports the conclusion. A strengthener on a weaken question is a classic trap.

CORRECT. Rising sales at Varda stores right across the border suggest Ostrel residents are still buying, just outside Ostrel. And falling sales at Varda's other stores suggest demand was dropping across the region anyway. Varda's flat total hid both, so Ostrel's 30 percent store decline overstates what the tax did to consumption.

questions.stimulus: All of the films nominated for this year’s Harrow Prize are documentaries. About half of the films shown at this year’s Leland Festival are documentaries. And some of this year’s documentaries received funding from the National Arts Council. So some films that received Arts Council funding were nominated for the Harrow Prize, and some were shown at the Leland Festival.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every member of the chess club also belongs to the math club. Most members of the math club are seniors. So most members of the chess club are seniors.

All of the restaurants on Pine Street serve vegetarian dishes. About half of the restaurants in the harbor district serve vegetarian dishes. And some restaurants that serve vegetarian dishes received a city health award. So some award-winning restaurants are on Pine Street, and some are in the harbor district.

All of the paintings in the museum’s east gallery are oil paintings, and about half of those in its west gallery are. Every oil painting in the museum is insured. So all of the east gallery’s paintings and at least half of the west gallery’s paintings are insured.
Some of the volunteers at the animal shelter are teachers, and some teachers in town donate to the shelter. So some of the shelter’s volunteers donate to the shelter.

All of the novels on this year’s prize shortlist were written in English. About half of the novels in the town library were written in English. So about half of the novels in the town library are on the prize shortlist.
questions.explanation: The original has all A are C, about half of B are C, some C are D, and concludes that some D are A and some D are B, ignoring that the C’s that are D might be neither A nor B. B repeats this exactly. C has the same opening but is valid because every C is insured, and D commits a different ‘some–some’ error with only two groups.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some Arts Council–funded films were Harrow nominees, and some were shown at Leland.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All Harrow nominees are documentaries; about half of Leland films are documentaries; some documentaries got Arts Council funding.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are C; about half of B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some D are B.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the gap? 'Some documentaries' got funding, but which ones? They could be documentaries that were neither nominated nor shown at Leland. There are lots of documentaries in the world. 'Some' isn't 'all': the members you care about could be the other ones. This is an overlap fallacy: two groups each overlap with C, and some C have a feature, so we're told both groups get the feature. We need the same three-part setup with a 'some' link and a double conclusion.

choices.note: A different flaw. This one passes 'most' through an 'all' link: chess club members could be the non-senior minority of the math club. It has no 'some C are D' step and no double conclusion.

CORRECT. All Pine Street restaurants serve vegetarian (all A are C); about half of harbor restaurants do (half B are C); some vegetarian-serving restaurants won (some C are D); so some winners are on Pine Street and some in the harbor district. Same pattern, same flaw: the winners could be vegetarian-serving restaurants on neither street.

Tempting. The first two sentences match the original almost word for word. But then it says EVERY oil painting is insured, not 'some.' That makes the argument valid. You can't match a flawed argument with a valid one.

Flawed, but differently. It links two groups through one 'some–some' overlap with teachers. The original has three groups and two conclusions, and its trouble comes from an 'all' and a 'half' feeding into a 'some.'
A different flaw. It treats sharing a trait (written in English) as membership in the shortlist. There's no 'some C are D' step at all.

questions.stimulus: Historical linguist: Some scholars claim that the Vessan language descended from Old Orrin, and as evidence they cite several dozen words that the two languages share. But shared words can easily arise through borrowing between neighboring peoples, and the Vessans and the Orrin speakers lived side by side for centuries. Thus, Vessan did not descend from Old Orrin.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the historical linguist’s reasoning?
choices: It treats the fact that the scholars’ evidence can be explained without their hypothesis as establishing that their hypothesis is false.
It presumes, without providing justification, that peoples who live side by side always borrow words from each other.
It relies on the testimony of scholars whose expertise in Old Orrin has not been established.
It takes for granted that any two languages that share words must have been spoken by neighboring peoples.
It fails to consider that borrowing between neighboring peoples could explain the words the two languages share.
questions.explanation: Showing that the shared words might come from borrowing only shows that the scholars’ evidence doesn’t prove descent; it doesn’t show descent didn’t happen, yet the linguist concludes it didn’t, as A says. B is attractive because borrowing is central, but the linguist says borrowing ‘can easily arise,’ not that it always occurs, and E describes the very point the linguist does consider.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Vessan did not descend from Old Orrin.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The scholars’ evidence is shared words; shared words can easily come from borrowing; the two peoples lived side by side for centuries.

breakdown.analysis: The linguist did something reasonable: showed the scholars' evidence is weak, because borrowing could explain the shared words. Then the linguist jumped to the opposite claim: Vessan definitely did not descend from Old Orrin. Knocking down an argument isn't the same as proving its conclusion false. Maybe Vessan did descend from Old Orrin and also borrowed words. It's like saying: your proof that it will rain is bad, so it won't rain. This is 'rebutting an argument treated as proving its conclusion false.' Know it. We need an answer that says the linguist treats a weakened case as a disproved one.

choices.note: CORRECT. Borrowing gives an alternative explanation of the shared words, which means the evidence doesn't establish descent. The linguist treats that as proof descent didn't happen. Undermining evidence isn't disproving the claim.

Tempting, because borrowing is the linguist's whole point. But the linguist says shared words 'can easily arise' through borrowing, not that neighbors always borrow. The argument doesn't presume 'always.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Neighboring towns always copy each other's festivals, so the two towns' identical parades must be copied.

choices.note: The linguist doesn't rely on the scholars at all; the linguist argues against them. There's no appeal to their authority.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: A famous physicist says Vessan came from Old Orrin, so it must have.

choices.note: Reversed. The linguist says neighbors can produce shared words, not that shared words require neighbors.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: These two languages share words, so their speakers must have lived next to each other.

choices.note: Contradicts the stimulus. Borrowing is exactly what the linguist considers. The problem is what the linguist concludes from it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Two languages share words, so they must be related. (ignoring borrowing)

questions.stimulus: Dietitian: Patients at the Ardley clinic who switched from eating white rice to eating brown rice reported that they felt full for longer after meals. Brown rice contains much more fiber than white rice does, and fiber slows digestion. So the extra fiber in brown rice is probably what made these patients feel full for longer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the dietitian’s argument?
choices: Brown rice contains somewhat more protein than white rice does, and protein also promotes a feeling of fullness.
Most of the patients who switched to brown rice said they preferred its taste to that of white rice.
Some patients at the clinic who did not switch to brown rice also reported feeling full for longer after meals.
Patients who kept eating white rice but added a fiber supplement equal to the extra fiber in brown rice also reported feeling full for longer.
Fiber has a number of health benefits in addition to slowing digestion.
questions.explanation: D isolates fiber: patients who got the extra fiber without switching rice also felt fuller, which supports fiber as the cause. A is the strongest trap in the wrong direction, since it offers protein as a rival explanation, and C suggests the fullness may not depend on brown rice at all.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extra fiber in brown rice probably made patients feel full longer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Patients who switched to brown rice felt full longer; brown rice has much more fiber; fiber slows digestion.

breakdown.analysis: Brown rice differs from white rice in more than fiber. Why credit the fiber specifically? To strengthen, isolate it: give people the fiber without the brown rice and see if they feel fuller. It's like figuring out whether a new mattress or a new pillow fixed your back pain: try the pillow alone. We need an answer that shows fiber alone produces the effect, or that rules out the other differences.

choices.note: Tempting because it's about fullness. But it names a rival cause, protein. That weakens the claim that fiber is what did it.
Irrelevant. Liking the taste doesn't explain feeling full longer, and it says nothing about fiber.
This hurts, if anything. If people who didn't switch also felt fuller, something other than brown rice may be at work.
CORRECT. Same white rice, plus the fiber, and patients felt full longer. That isolates fiber as the cause.
So? Other benefits of fiber don't show that fiber caused the fullness here.

questions.stimulus: Film archivist: The only surviving print of the 1931 film The Pale Orchard is deteriorating and will be unwatchable within a decade. Making a high-resolution digital copy of the print would cost far less than restoring it chemically, and a digital copy would preserve the film’s images indefinitely. So the archive should digitize the print rather than restore it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the film archivist’s argument depends?
choices: Most people who watch old films prefer to watch digital copies rather than projected prints.
The archive’s budget is too small to pay for a chemical restoration of the print.
Making a high-resolution digital copy of the print would not require that the print first be restored chemically.
A chemical restoration would keep the print watchable for no more than another decade.
A digital copy of The Pale Orchard would be viewed more often than the restored print would be.
questions.explanation: The archivist presents digitizing as an alternative to restoring; if a usable digital copy could be made only from a chemically restored print, the choice ‘digitize rather than restore’ would make no sense, so C is required. D is tempting, but the argument already says a digital copy lasts indefinitely, so a restoration lasting longer than a decade would not undercut it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The archive should digitize the print rather than restore it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The print will be unwatchable within a decade; digitizing costs far less than chemical restoration; a digital copy preserves the images indefinitely.

breakdown.analysis: Digitize rather than restore: that treats them as separate options. But what if the print is too damaged to scan well unless it's restored first? Then digitizing isn't an alternative to restoring; it depends on it, and the cost comparison falls apart. We need an answer that says digitizing doesn't require restoring the print first. Negation test: if digitizing requires restoration, 'digitize rather than restore' is impossible.

choices.note: Not required. The argument is about cost and preservation, not viewer taste. Negated, the case for digitizing still stands.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most viewers of old films prefer digital copies.

choices.note: Not required. The argument says digitizing is cheaper and preserves the images longer. Even if the archive could afford restoration, those reasons still favor digitizing.
choices.negation: The archive’s budget is large enough to pay for a chemical restoration.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, digitizing requires restoring the print first. Then the archive can't digitize instead of restoring, and the cost advantage disappears. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Making a high-resolution digital copy would require that the print first be restored chemically.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like it backs the comparison. But a digital copy already lasts indefinitely, so even if restoration lasted twenty or thirty years, digitizing would still win. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: A chemical restoration would keep the print watchable for more than another decade.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How often people watch each version isn't one of the archivist's reasons. Negated, the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: A digital copy would not be viewed more often than the restored print.
